Kerry did not sleep that night either, and this time he did not pretend he was going to. He lay in the dark with the chest closed across the room, and he listened to the room the way you listen to a house you have just moved into, trying to learn which sounds are the house and which sounds are not.

At 1:07, the watch ticked. At 2:07, it ticked. At 3:07, the knocking came back, three knocks, a pause, three knocks, from the inside of the chest, and Joshua sat straight up with his hand over his mouth, and Kerry got up, because staying in bed felt like waiting, and waiting felt like agreeing.

"Don't open it," Joshua said from the bed.

"I'm not opening it," Kerry said. "I'm counting."

He counted out loud, because counting out loud felt like taking the counting back. "One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six."

The knocking stopped.

"See?" Kerry said. "It stops at six. It never gets to seven on its own. It needs somebody to say seven for it."

"Then don't say seven," Joshua said.

Kerry did not say seven. He went back to bed, and he lay there with his eyes open, and at 4:07, the photograph changed again. He knew because he opened the chest at 4:06, just to check, just to make sure the things were still in their row. The things were still in their row. The photograph was still dated tomorrow.

Only now, in the photograph, there were seven people standing in front of the chest. Kerry counted them twice, because counting is what you do when you do not trust your eyes. Two of them were him and Joshua. Four of them were strangers, two men and two women, standing in a row like a photograph taken at a reunion nobody had invited them to. And the seventh person was standing behind the mirror, where a reflection should not be able to stand, with no face Kerry could make out, only a shape, tall and patient, like a teacher who has all day and is not in a hurry to be understood.

He closed the chest. He closed it hard enough that the iron bands rang, a dull, flat sound, like a bell that has been buried.

In the morning, the seventh name on the list had grown. It was no longer just a K. It was K, and then, in the same dust-fine writing, an E, and then, by the time Kerry had made coffee he did not drink, an R.

"Kerr," Joshua said, reading over his shoulder. "Kerr. That's not a name. That's the start of a name."

"Or the start of your name," Joshua said, very quietly, a moment later, when he understood what he had said. "Kerry. K-E-R-R-Y. It's spelling your name, Kerry. It's spelling it one letter at a time, and when it finishes, the seventh name won't be blank anymore."

Kerry looked at the list. The third name was his own. The seventh name was becoming his own, too, letter by letter, and he did not know what that meant, except that it could not mean anything good, because nothing about the chest had meant anything good yet, and it had meant a great many things that were bad in very specific ways.

"We need to play the other things first," Kerry said, suddenly, the way a person says a thing they have only just understood. "The tape says PLAY ME LAST. Last means there are things to play before it. The key, the mirror, the watch, the photograph, the list, the envelope. Six things. Six things before the tape. The tape is the seventh thing you play, and we're on six, Kerry, we're always on six, because seven is the thing that finishes."

"So we play them," Joshua said. "In order. The way the chest laid them out. Photograph, key, tape — no, tape last. Photograph first. What does the photograph play?"

"The photograph plays tomorrow," Kerry said. "It plays what hasn't happened yet. That's why it's dated tomorrow. It's not a photograph of what was. It's a photograph of what will be, if we keep going the way we're going."

"The key?" Joshua asked.

Kerry picked up the key with seven teeth. It was cold, colder than the chest. He held it up to the light, and the light went through it in a way light should not go through metal, and for a second, he saw, in the key, not his room, but a corridor, and a door, and a number on the door.

"Seven," Kerry said. "The key doesn't open the chest. The chest has no lock. The key opens something else. Something with a door marked seven. Something we haven't found yet."

"The mirror?" Joshua asked.

"The mirror plays us," Kerry said. "Late. A half-second late. It's playing us back, so it can learn to be us."

"The watch?"

"The watch plays time," Kerry said. "It stopped at seven-oh-seven, and it ticks on the seven, every hour, because it's counting down to seven-oh-seven, and when it gets there, it won't tick anymore. It'll chime. Or it'll open. Or it'll finish."

"The list?"

"The list plays the people who came before us," Kerry said. "Elias Hart. June Calloway. Marcus Webb. Delia Frost. And us. And one more."

"The envelope?"

Kerry picked up the envelope. It was empty now. He had opened it in Chapter 1, and the paper inside had said, in his own handwriting, YOU OPENED IT. NOW IT KNOWS YOUR NAME. Now the envelope was empty, and the paper was gone, and Kerry understood, suddenly, why the envelope had been sealed with black wax and addressed to him and to no one else.

"The envelope played me," Kerry said. "It played me the first night. It told me it knows my name, and now it's writing my name on the list, letter by letter, and when it finishes, I won't be the third name anymore. I'll be the seventh name, too. I'll be the one who opens, and the one who is opened. I'll be the one who finishes."

Joshua took Kerry's hand. His hand was shaking, but he didn't let go.

"Then we don't finish," Joshua said. "That's the rule. That's the only rule that matters. We don't play the tape. We don't say seven. We don't let it finish. We keep it on six, forever, if we have to."

At 7:07 that evening, the watch did not tick. It chimed. One chime, low and patient, like a bell that has been buried and is finally allowed to ring.

And the chest, which was closed, which Joshua had closed with both hands, opened itself, slowly, without a sound, the way a door opens when somebody on the other side has been waiting for you to knock.

Inside, the seven things were still in their row, except for one thing, which was no longer in its row.

The cassette tape was sitting on top of the chest, outside it, in the middle of the floor, where neither of them had put it.

And on its label, in the same thin blue ink, underneath PLAY ME LAST, there was now a second line, written in handwriting Kerry recognized, because it was his own:

PLAY ME NOW.

"We don't play it," Joshua said.

"I know," Kerry said.

"We played the other six," Joshua said. "That's what it wanted. It wanted us to play the other six, so we'd get to the tape, so we'd think playing the tape was our idea."

"I know," Kerry said.

"We don't play it," Joshua said again, because saying a rule out loud is sometimes the only way to keep it.

Kerry picked up the tape.

"Kerry," Joshua said.

"Just a look," Kerry said. "Just to see if there's anything else written on it. Just —"

The tape was warm. Not warm like a living thing. Warm like a thing that has been sitting in the sun, except there was no sun, and it was evening, and the room was dark, and the chest was open, and the tape was sitting in the middle of the floor where neither of them had put it.

Joshua sat down on the bed. He did not get up. He did not move at all, which told Kerry more about how scared Joshua was than any shouting could have.

"Talk me out of it," Kerry said.

"I can't," Joshua said. "Because if I talk you out of it, it'll just wait. It waited for Elias Hart. It waited for June Calloway. It waited for Marcus Webb and Delia Frost. It waited for us. Waiting is what it does best. And while it waits, it's spelling your name on the list, one letter at a time, and when it finishes, it'll be done whether we play the tape or not."

Kerry looked at the list. The seventh name was now K-E-R-R. Four letters. One letter left.

"So we play it on our terms," Kerry said. "In daylight. With the window open and the door unlocked. Together. That's the rule. That's the only rule that matters."

They did not have a cassette player. Nobody had a cassette player anymore, except for one man, three blocks away, who ran a repair shop out of a storefront with a sign that said WE FIX ANYTHING, and who looked at the tape the way a man looks at a thing he has seen before and hoped never to see again.

"I don't want it in my shop," the man said.

"We'll pay you," Kerry said.

"It's not about pay," the man said. "It's about what it plays. I had one of these once. It played my voice, saying things I hadn't said yet. I threw it in the river. The river gave it back."

He fixed them a player anyway, because Kerry paid him, and because Joshua asked him, quietly, without making a speech out of it, and because the man understood, the way people who have been down on their luck understand each other, that sometimes you do a thing for a person not because it's safe, but because it's the only thing left to do.

Back in the room, with the window open and the door unlocked, Kerry put the tape in the player, and Joshua took Kerry's hand, and Kerry pressed play, because pressing play was the only way to find out what PLAY ME LAST had been waiting to say.

First, there was their own voice. Kerry's voice, and Joshua's voice, talking over each other, laughing, saying words they had said that afternoon in the storage corridor, word for word, including the part where Joshua said, "That's what people say right before a horror movie starts," and Kerry said, "There is no music," and Joshua said, "Exactly."

Then there was the night. The counting. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. And then a pause, long enough for Kerry to understand that a pause can be the worst part of a sound, because a pause is where you wait for the thing you already know is coming.

Then there was the third voice. Low and patient, like a teacher who has all day and is not in a hurry to be understood.

"Seven," the third voice said. "Seven is listening."

And then, for the first time, the third voice said more than seven. It said, slowly, clearly, as if it were reading from a list, the names Kerry already knew, in order, one by one.

"Elias Hart. June Calloway. Kerry Lewis. Marcus Webb. Delia Frost. Joshua Byrd."

Six names. Six names, and then a pause, long enough for Kerry to understand that a pause can be the worst part of a sound.

And then the third voice said the seventh name, and it was not Kerry's name, and it was not Joshua's name, and it was not any name Kerry had ever heard before, and yet, when he heard it, he knew it the way you know a face in a photograph dated tomorrow.

"Yara," the third voice said. "Yara is seventh."

Kerry stopped the tape. His hands were shaking, but he didn't let go of Joshua's hand.

"Yara," Joshua said. "Who is Yara?"

"I don't know," Kerry said. "But the list is spelling my name, and the tape is saying Yara, and those two things can't both be true, unless —"

Unless the list was not spelling his name. Unless K-E-R-R was the start of a different name. Unless the seventh name was not his, and had never been his, and the chest had only wanted him to think it was, because fear is a faster animal than good sense, and it had already gotten its teeth into him.

At 7:07, the watch chimed again. At 7:07, the knocking came back, three knocks, a pause, three knocks, and this time, the knocking was not on the inside of the chest.

It was on the door.

Kerry and Joshua looked at each other. The door was unlocked, because that was the rule, because they had promised themselves they would not open a strange cold chest at night, and they had promised themselves they would not play the tape, and they had broken both promises, and now somebody was knocking on their door, at seven-oh-seven, in the exact rhythm of the chest.

Three knocks. A pause. Three knocks.

"Don't answer it," Joshua whispered, which made no sense, because nobody had asked a question, but in the dark it felt like the right thing to say.

Kerry got up. He got up because staying on the bed felt like waiting, and waiting felt like agreeing. He crossed the room in his bare feet, and the floor was cold under his feet in a way the floor had never been cold before, and he put his hand on the door.

"Who is it?" Kerry asked.

There was no answer. There was only a pause, long enough for Kerry to understand that a pause can be the worst part of a sound.

And then, from the other side of the door, in a voice that was neither Kerry's nor Joshua's, low and patient, like a teacher who has all day and is not in a hurry to be understood, came a single word, spoken the way a person speaks their own name when they are introducing themselves for the first time.

"Yara."

Kerry did not open the door. Not yet. He stood with his hand on the door, and Joshua stood behind him, with his hand on Kerry's shoulder, and the tape, which Kerry had stopped, started playing again on its own, very faint, very far away, like a radio in another apartment with the wall too thin.

And on the tape, the third voice said, for the last time that night, the only thing it had left to say, the thing it had been counting toward since the first night in Unit 7, since the first photograph dated tomorrow, since the first time Kerry had put his hand on a cold chest and pulled it back fast:

"Seven is here."

And underneath it, in the room, in the chest, on the list, the seventh name finished spelling itself, letter by letter, in dust-fine writing, in handwriting Kerry did not recognize and Joshua said he did not recognize either, and the name it spelled was not Kerry's, and it was not Joshua's, and it was not a name either of them had ever seen before, except on a photograph dated tomorrow, in a room they had not yet walked into, standing behind a mirror where a reflection should not be able to stand.

YARA.

Horror Comedy · All 250 Chapters Out Now

DEAD END

A horror comedy based on true events — 250 chapters. Kerry and Joshua, down on their luck in Hollywood, turn down a street that has no way out, and the street starts laughing back. A dead phone, a move-along at dawn, a cop who keeps saying the same thing, and a clock stuck at 5:12.

Chapter 1 — The Sign Says Dead EndPublished October 28, 2026 · Read

The cop was polite about it, which somehow made it worse.

"Sir, you gotta move along. You can't stay here."

Kerry had heard that sentence so many times he could have said it with him, in harmony, like a duet nobody asked for. He had heard it at dawn, at midnight, at that weird hour that is technically morning but feels like a rumor. He had heard it from cops who meant it kindly and cops who meant it like a threat and cops who were just tired, the way everybody in Hollywood is tired at 5 a.m., even the palm trees.

"I'm moving," Kerry said. "I'm literally in the process of moving. This is me, moving."

He was not moving. He was sitting on a curb with a backpack, a phone at 2%, and a blanket that had seen things. Joshua was already up, already folding their tent with the speed of a man who has folded a tent in the dark more times than he has folded a fitted sheet in his entire life, which is to say, a lot.

"Two minutes," Joshua said. "That's all I need. Two minutes and we're ghosts."

"Ghosts don't have to move along," Kerry said. "That's the whole point of being a ghost. No rent, no rules, no 5 a.m. wake-up call from a man with a flashlight and a clipboard."

The cop pretended not to hear that. Cops in Hollywood are very good at pretending not to hear things. It might be their main skill, right after standing.

They moved. That is what you do. You move, you find a new spot, you tell yourself this spot is better, quieter, safer, and then at some hour that is not a real hour, somebody with a flashlight tells you to move again. It is a dance. Nobody taught Kerry the steps. He learned them the way you learn anything on the street: by stepping on everybody's feet, including your own.

This time, though, the move went wrong in a new way.

They turned left instead of right — Joshua's idea, which he would later deny with great confidence — and left turned into a side street, and the side street turned into an alley, and the alley turned into something Kerry had never seen before in a city he thought he knew by heart.

A dead end.

Not a metaphor. A real one. A street that just stopped, like it had run out of ideas. At the end of it, under a streetlight that was flickering in a rhythm that was almost, but not quite, a song, there was a sign.

DEAD END.

Kerry stared at it. Joshua stared at it. The sign, being a sign, stared back in the way only a sign can, which is to say, it did nothing at all, and somehow that was the creepiest part.

"I've lived in this neighborhood for years," Kerry said. "I have walked every street in Hollywood. I have been moved along from every street in Hollywood. I have never seen this street."

"Maybe it's new," Joshua said.

"Streets don't just appear, Joshua."

"Tell that to the street."

Fair point. Kerry hated when Joshua had a fair point before coffee. Coffee, it should be noted, was also a rumor at this hour. The nearest place that sold coffee was closed, and the nearest place that gave coffee away was, according to a man Kerry trusted, "ten minutes away," which in outreach time means anywhere from ten minutes to the heat death of the universe.

Kerry's phone buzzed its last warning. 2%. Then 1%. Then, with the drama of a soap opera star, it died. The screen went black, and Kerry held it up like a man holding a dead hamster and hoping for a miracle.

"Great," he said. "No phone, no charge, no map, and we're standing in a street that doesn't exist. This is fine. This is a completely normal Tuesday."

"It isn't Tuesday," Joshua said.

Kerry looked at him. "What day is it?"

Joshua thought about it. He thought about it for a long time, the way you think about a question when you realize you have lost track of something important, like what day it is, or where you left your keys, or when exactly your life became a series of 5 a.m. conversations with patient policemen.

"I don't know," Joshua said finally. "I think it was Tuesday yesterday. It might still be Tuesday. It might be Tuesday forever now."

And then, from somewhere at the end of the dead end, past the sign, past the flickering light, past the place where the street gave up, somebody laughed.

It was not a scary laugh. That was the scary part. It was a warm laugh, a real laugh, the kind of laugh you hear from a friend who has just heard a good joke. It sounded like somebody who knew Kerry, and liked him, and had been waiting for him to finally show up.

Kerry looked at Joshua. Joshua looked at Kerry.

"Did you hear that?" Kerry asked.

"Yes," Joshua said. "And before you ask: no, I do not want to go see what it was."

"Good," Kerry said. "Because I wasn't going to ask. I was going to tell you we're going to see what it was."

"Kerry."

"Joshua."

They stood there for a moment, two men at the end of a street that didn't exist, with a dead phone, a folded tent, and a laugh waiting for them in the dark like an invitation nobody should accept and everybody does.

"Okay," Joshua said, sighing the sigh of a man who knows he is about to do something stupid and has decided to do it with style. "But if something eats us, I'm blaming you."

"If something eats us," Kerry said, "I will accept full responsibility, in writing, just as soon as we are digested."

They walked toward the sign.

The streetlight stopped flickering. It went steady, bright, and warm, like a porch light left on for somebody coming home late.

And the laugh came again, closer this time, like it was glad to see them.

Kerry laughed back, because that is what you do when you are scared and you don't want anybody, including yourself, to know it. His laugh echoed down the dead end and came back sounding just a little bit different, like it had picked up a friend on the way.

Joshua grabbed his hand. "Don't let go," he said.

"I'm not planning to," Kerry said.

They stepped past the sign that said DEAD END, into the street that had no way out, and the city of Hollywood, which had spent years telling them to move along, finally, for the first time, told them to stay.

Not in words. In a laugh. In a light. In a street that was waiting.

And that, Kerry thought, as the dead end closed around them like a joke with a punchline he couldn't see yet, was either the worst decision he had ever made, or the beginning of the funniest, scariest, truest story he had ever lived.

Probably both.

Chapter 2 — Move AlongPublished October 28, 2026 · Read

The first thing Kerry noticed, once they were past the sign, was that the dead end was quiet in a way Hollywood never is.

Hollywood is never quiet. Even at 5 a.m., Hollywood hums. There is traffic somewhere, a siren somewhere, a man arguing with a parking meter about a ticket he definitely deserved. Hollywood is a city that talks in its sleep.

This street did not talk. This street listened.

"Okay," Joshua whispered, still holding Kerry's hand, which was good, because Kerry's hand was the only thing he was sure was still his. "New rule. We walk back out the way we came in, we find a real street, we find coffee, and we pretend this alley is a story we tell later, when we're safe and caffeinated and somebody else is paying for breakfast."

"Agreed," Kerry said. "One hundred percent agreed. Turning around now."

They turned around.

The sign was still there. DEAD END. Only now it was behind them, which meant they were already in it, which they knew, but seeing the sign from the other side made it worse, like reading a warning label after you already swallowed the thing.

And then, from the mouth of the alley, where the real street should have been, a flashlight clicked on.

"Sir," a voice said, polite as ever. "You gotta move along. You can't stay here."

Kerry froze. Joshua froze. The flashlight did not freeze. It swept across them, slow and professional, the way flashlights do when they belong to someone who has done this a thousand times and will do it a thousand more.

It was the same cop.

Same voice. Same flashlight. Same clipboard, somehow, even though Kerry was fairly sure clipboards do not appear out of thin air, and fairly sure this cop had not followed them, because they had watched him walk away, and because cops do not teleport, and because if cops could teleport, Hollywood would be a very different, much more efficient place.

"Didn't we just do this?" Kerry asked. It came out braver than he felt, which is the best kind of bravery, the accidental kind.

The cop tilted his head. "Sir?"

"We just moved along," Kerry said. "Five minutes ago. You told us to move along, we moved along, and we moved along right into here. So technically, we obeyed you. We are the most obedient people you have moved along all week. Possibly all year. You should put that in your report. 'Subjects complied immediately and with enthusiasm.'"

The cop did not smile. Cops on this job rarely smile at 5 a.m., and this cop was no exception, except that he was smiling a second ago, Kerry was sure of it, or no, wait, that was the other cop, the first cop, and this was the same cop, so how —

"Joshua," Kerry whispered. "Is this the same cop, or a different cop who looks exactly like the same cop?"

Joshua stared. "Kerry. It's the same cop. Same uniform. Same mustache. Same little scar on his chin where he probably cut himself shaving in 2019 and never forgave the razor."

"Thank you," Kerry said. "That's very specific and very unhelpful, but thank you."

"Sir," the cop said again, patient as a man reading a script he has read so many times the words have worn smooth. "You gotta move along. You can't stay here."

"Where is 'here'?" Kerry asked, because his mouth sometimes asks questions before his brain has approved them, and his brain was currently on strike. "Because out there, you told us we couldn't stay there. In here, you're telling us we can't stay here. So where, exactly, are we allowed to stay? Is there a list? Is there a map? Is there a brochure? I would love a brochure. A brochure with pictures. 'Welcome to Hollywood: Places You Are Allowed to Exist.'"

The cop looked at him for a long moment. Then he did something cops are not supposed to do in the middle of a move-along.

He laughed.

Not the warm laugh from the end of the street. A tired laugh. A human laugh. The laugh of a man who has heard every version of this argument and is still, somehow, on the job.

"Son," he said, and the word "son" did something strange to Kerry's chest, because nobody had called him that in a long time, and because it sounded, for just a second, like it came from somewhere else, somewhere older, somewhere that was not a dead-end alley at dawn. "There isn't a list. There's just moving. That's the job. You move, I move, everybody moves, and eventually everybody ends up somewhere. That's how the city works."

"And if we don't move?" Joshua asked quietly.

The cop's flashlight dipped, just a little, like he was tired of holding it up, like he was tired of a lot of things.

"Then you stay," he said. "And staying is how you end up in places like this."

He clicked the flashlight off. The alley went dark for half a second, and in that half a second, Kerry heard the warm laugh again, closer, from behind them this time, from deep in the dead end, and he heard Joshua's breath catch, and he heard his own heart doing something it had not done in a long time, which was beating fast for a reason that was not fear, exactly, but was not not fear either.

When the light came back — not the flashlight, the streetlight, steady and warm — the cop was gone.

Not walked away gone. Gone gone. The mouth of the alley was empty. The real street was out there, somewhere, with its traffic and its sirens and its men arguing with parking meters, but from inside the dead end, it looked very far away, like a television left on in another room.

"Okay," Joshua said, very calmly, in the voice of a man who is about to be very not calm. "So. The same cop. The same speech. Twice. In a street that doesn't exist. And now he's gone, and we're still here, and my phone says it's 5:12, and your phone is dead, and my phone has been saying 5:12 for —"

He looked at his phone. He looked at it again. He turned it toward Kerry.

5:12.

"It was 5:12 when we got here," Joshua said. "It was 5:12 when the cop showed up the first time. It was 5:12 when he showed up the second time. Kerry, what time is it?"

Kerry looked up at the sky. The sky over the dead end was not dawn and not night. It was a color Kerry did not have a name for, a color between, like the sky was still deciding.

"I don't know," Kerry said. "But I think we're about to find out why this street is called a dead end."

"Why?" Joshua asked. "Because it ends?"

"No," Kerry said, and he squeezed Joshua's hand, and he laughed, because laughing was the only thing left that felt like his. "Because it doesn't. Because it never ends. Because you can move along all you want in a dead end, and you will always, always end up right back here, at 5:12, with the same cop, telling you the same thing, forever."

The warm laugh answered him from the dark, like applause.

"Great," Joshua said. "So we're stuck in a loop, in a dead end, with a ghost cop and a laughing street. On the bright side, at least nobody can move us along anymore. We're already as moved along as it's possible to be."

"That's the spirit," Kerry said. "Now let's go find out who's laughing, before 5:12 happens again."

They walked deeper into the dead end, hand in hand, past the sign that had already done its job, toward a laugh that sounded, more and more, like it was glad they had stayed.

Behind them, at the mouth of the alley, a flashlight clicked on, just once, like a wink.

And a polite voice, very far away and very close at the same time, said: "Sir. You gotta move along."

Kerry did not turn around. He had already heard that line twice. The third time, he decided, he would answer it.

Next time, he would ask the cop to stay.

Chapter 3 — The Tent That Wasn't There YesterdayPublished October 28, 2026 · Read

The first thing Kerry did, once the laughing had settled back into the walls and the streetlight had stopped showing off, was try to find their spot again.

That is what you do when you have been moved along. You do not look for a new life. You look for the old curb. You look for the place where your tent was, where your blanket was, where you had finally, after three tries and one very loud argument about which way was north, gotten the poles to behave.

"Left," Joshua said. "I think it was left."

"It was not left," Kerry said. "It was left-ish. There is a difference, and that difference is currently the entire reason we are lost."

They walked left-ish.

And there it was.

Their tent.

Same color, same sag on the left side where the pole had given up pretending to be straight, same dent in the rainfly where Joshua had once leaned on it too hard while reaching for a phone charger and had declared, with great dignity, that the tent had attacked him first.

Kerry stopped so fast Joshua nearly walked into his back.

"That's our tent," Kerry said.

Joshua stared. "Kerry. We folded our tent. I folded it. I am very good at folding tents. I folded it in the dark, in under two minutes, while a policeman watched me, which is a level of performance pressure most people never experience."

"I know," Kerry said. "I watched you do it. You were magnificent. You were a tent-folding Olympian. And yet."

"And yet," Joshua said, "there is our tent, standing up, like it never got folded at all, like it slept in and decided to stay home."

They walked closer, slowly, the way you walk toward a dog you are not sure is friendly. The tent did not move. Tents rarely do, unless the wind is feeling ambitious, and there was no wind in the dead end. There was not even a breeze. The air in the dead end was the kind of still that makes you check whether you are still breathing, just to be polite.

Kerry crouched down and looked at the seam on the front flap.

There it was. The patch.

A small, crooked square of fabric, sewn on with thread that did not quite match, in stitches that were not quite straight, because Joshua sews the way he does everything else in a hurry: fast, confident, and slightly off-center in a way that is, somehow, perfect.

"Joshua," Kerry said, very quietly. "That is your patch."

Joshua crouched beside him. He touched the patch with two fingers, like it might be hot. "I sewed that patch," he said. "I sewed it last winter. I remember because I complained the entire time. I said, 'Why am I sewing a tent in winter, this is not what I signed up for,' and you said, 'You signed up for everything, that's what being with me is,' and I said —"

"You said, 'Fair, but I'm still complaining,'" Kerry finished.

"Exactly," Joshua said. "Nobody else sews a patch like that. Nobody else complains while sewing a patch like that. That patch is mine the way a fingerprint is mine."

"So," Kerry said, "either somebody stole our tent, unfolded it, and set it up here before we got here, which would require time travel and a truly impressive commitment to a prank —"

"Or," Joshua said, "this tent was here yesterday. And it wasn't here yesterday. Both. At the same time."

Kerry looked at the tent. The tent looked at Kerry, in the way only a tent can, which is to say, it did nothing at all, and somehow that was the creepiest part, and Kerry was starting to notice a pattern in this street: the creepiest part was always the part that did nothing at all.

"Okay," Kerry said. "Decision time. Do we claim it, or do we walk past our own life like it belongs to somebody else?"

Joshua thought about it. He thought about it the way he thinks about everything important: out loud, in a circle, until the circle lands somewhere useful.

"If we claim it," he said, "we are saying this street gets to give us back our stuff, and we are grateful, and we will stay for more gifts. If we walk past it, we are saying we don't need the street's charity, and we keep walking, and we sleep on concrete, which I have done, and I can tell you, concrete has no lumbar support."

"Claim it," Kerry said. "But carefully. Like you would claim a dog that might be somebody else's dog. Politely. With an exit plan."

They unzipped the tent.

Inside was their blanket. The blanket that had seen things. Folded neatly, which neither of them had ever done, because folding a blanket neatly requires a belief in tomorrow that, at 5:12 in the morning, neither of them had ever quite managed.

Under the blanket was a note.

Kerry picked it up. The handwriting was his own. He knew it the way you know your own laugh in a recording: a little embarrassed, a little surprised, and completely certain.

The note said: *You left this here yesterday. You will leave it here tomorrow. Don't worry about which yesterday. — K.*

Joshua read it over his shoulder. "Kerry," he said. "Did you write that?"

"I don't remember writing that," Kerry said. "But I also don't remember not writing it. And that, somehow, is worse."

He folded the note and put it in his pocket, because in the dead end, you keep the notes. Notes are currency here, or clues, or jokes, and Kerry was not yet sure which, but he was sure you did not throw them away.

"So we're staying in our own tent," Joshua said, "which is not our tent, in a street that is not a street, on a day that might be yesterday."

"Yes," Kerry said, crawling in. "And for the first time since we got moved along, we have a roof. Even if the roof is ours, and also not ours, and also yesterday's. I'll take it."

Joshua crawled in after him. The tent smelled like their tent. It smelled like rain and laundry soap and the faint, stubborn hope that tomorrow would be a little easier than today.

Outside, the warm laugh came again, soft, like applause from the next room.

"You're welcome," Kerry said to the dark, because manners cost nothing, even in a dead end. "But next time, leave a coffee too."

The laugh, Kerry could have sworn, sounded pleased with itself.

He fell asleep holding Joshua's hand, in a tent that wasn't there yesterday, in a street that didn't exist, at a time that refused to move.

And for one whole, impossible night, nobody told him to move along.

That, more than the tent, more than the note, more than the laugh, was the strangest thing of all.

Chapter 4 — Charging at 2%Published October 28, 2026 · Read

Kerry woke up to the sound of his own phone dying a second time, which is a sentence that should not make sense and, in the dead end, made perfect sense.

His phone had died in Chapter 1. It had died dramatically, at 2%, then 1%, then black. Now it buzzed, weakly, like a man clearing his throat before delivering bad news.

2%.

Again.

"Joshua," Kerry said, holding up the phone. "My phone is at 2% again. It died, and now it's at 2% again. That's not charging. That's haunting."

Joshua's phone was worse. Joshua's phone had been at 5:12 for so long that the numbers had started to feel less like a time and more like a name. 5:12. Like a neighbor. Like a roommate who never pays rent and never leaves.

"We need a charge," Joshua said. "We need a real charge, not a ghost charge, not a loop charge, not a 'your phone is at 2% forever and you will never know why' charge."

"Agreed," Kerry said. "Find me a plug, and I will be your best friend for life. Find me two plugs, and I will be your best friend for two lives."

The dead end, helpful as ever, provided a man.

He appeared at the mouth of their tent — not walked up, appeared, the way people appear in the dead end, which is to say, one moment he was not there, and the next moment he was there, holding a power strip like it was a bouquet of flowers.

"Morning," the man said. He was older, or younger, Kerry couldn't tell, because the dead end did bad things to ages. "You boys need a charge?"

"Yes," Kerry said, too fast. "Yes, please, God, yes, we need a charge, we have been at 2% since the dawn of time, or at least since Tuesday, which might be the same thing here."

The man smiled. He had a kind smile, which in the dead end was either a good sign or a warning, and Kerry had not yet learned which.

"One charge," the man said, plugging the strip into nothing. Kerry watched the plug go into the air, or into a wall that wasn't there, or into something Kerry's eyes refused to report accurately. "One charge each. Price is not money."

Kerry froze, phone halfway out of his pocket. "Not money," he repeated. "Okay. I like where this is going, and I also hate where this is going. What is the price, if it's not money?"

"A story," the man said. "A true one. One you haven't told anybody else today."

Joshua laughed. "That's it? A story? Kerry, we have stories. We have stories coming out of our ears. We have stories we haven't even told each other yet, and we tell each other everything, except the things we are saving for dramatic effect."

"Careful," the man said, still smiling. "A story here is not free. You tell it, and it leaves you. Not forgotten — left. Like you gave it away, and now it lives here, in the street, and the street can tell it to somebody else, on a night when somebody else needs it."

Kerry looked at Joshua. Joshua looked at Kerry. This was, Kerry realized, the dead end's first real rule, even if nobody had written it down yet: everything here costs a story, not cash.

Cash was easy. Cash you could count. Cash you could run out of and then borrow and then run out of again. Stories were different. Stories were yours in a way cash never was. Giving away a story felt like giving away a piece of furniture from a house you were still living in. You could do it. You just had to decide which chair you could live without.

"Okay," Kerry said. "I'll pay. One story. A true one. About the first time I got moved along and laughed about it anyway, because if I hadn't laughed, I would have cried, and crying at 5 a.m. in front of a policeman is a level of vulnerability I was not prepared for."

He told it. It was short, it was true, and it was funny in the way true things are funny when you tell them after enough time has passed to make them safe.

The man listened, nodding, and when Kerry finished, the man plugged Kerry's phone into the strip that was plugged into nothing, and the phone lit up.

3%. Then 10%. Then 27%. Then, like it was showing off, 48%.

Kerry gasped. "It's charging. It's actually charging. Joshua, it's charging, I can feel it in my soul, I can feel it in my —"

"My turn," Joshua said, stepping forward. "I pay with a story too. A true one. About the time Kerry tried to fold a fitted sheet and declared war on the sheet, and the sheet won, and Kerry said the sheet had cheated."

Joshua told it. The man laughed, a real laugh, and plugged Joshua's phone in, and Joshua's phone climbed too, past 5:12 — no, wait, the time still said 5:12, because the clock was still stuck, but the battery climbed, and that was enough, that was more than enough.

"Thank you," Kerry said, holding his phone like a newborn. "Seriously. Thank you. What do I call you?"

The man packed up his power strip. "People here call me whatever story they paid with. Today, you can call me the Fitted Sheet Man, if you like."

"We like," Joshua said. "We like that very much."

The man walked away, or disappeared, or turned a corner that Kerry was fairly sure had not been there a second ago. Kerry did not chase him. In the dead end, you did not chase the help. You thanked the help, and you kept the charge, and you remembered the price.

That night, Kerry tried to tell Joshua the move-along story again, just to hear it, just to make sure it was still his.

He could tell it. He remembered it. But it sounded different now, like a song somebody else had covered. Like it belonged to the street a little bit, and to him a little bit, and to whoever needed it next, a little bit more.

"Is that bad?" Joshua asked, in the dark, at 5:12.

"No," Kerry said, after a long time. "I think that's how stories work here. You don't lose them by telling them. You just share the rent."

He plugged his phone in again, out of habit, even though there was no plug, and the phone, loyal as ever, said 48%.

In the dead end, Kerry was learning, 48% was a fortune.

And a story was the only money that never ran out, because the more you told it, the more of it there was to tell.

Chapter 5 — The Man With the CartPublished October 28, 2026 · Read

The cart came with a bell, which is how Kerry knew it was trouble, because in his experience, good news does not need a bell.

It rolled down the dead end at exactly 5:12 — Kerry checked, Joshua checked, the clock on the wall of a building that had not had a clock yesterday checked, and they were all in agreement, which was rare and therefore suspicious — and it stopped in front of their tent like it had been heading there all along.

The man pushing it was not the charging man. This man was different. He was older, or younger, or both, in the way the dead end did ages. He wore an apron with too many pockets, and every pocket was full of something that rattled, or hummed, or refused to explain itself.

"Morning," he said, ringing his bell once, politely, like a man announcing a train that is only going to his own imagination. "New stock today. Fresh in. Never used, mostly."

"Mostly?" Kerry asked.

"Mostly never used," the man said. "Some things have been used by people who do not remember using them, which is almost the same as never used, except for the memories, which are extra, no charge."

Joshua peered at the cart. It was full of impossible inventory: a phone charger that fit no phone Kerry had ever owned, and no phone Joshua had ever owned, and possibly no phone that had ever been manufactured on Earth. A map, folded into a shape that was not quite a square, showing streets that did not exist, with names like Almost Avenue and Sorry Street and, right in the middle, the dead end itself, drawn in gold ink, like it was proud of itself.

A key with no lock. A lock with no key. A pair of sunglasses for a night that never got dark enough to need them, and a pair of gloves for a summer that never got cold enough to need them, and a small, brass compass that pointed, stubbornly, at Kerry.

"That compass is pointing at me," Kerry said.

"It does that," the man said. "It points at whoever needs it most, which today is you, which is flattering and also a little rude, if you think about it."

Kerry bought nothing. He had no cash, and in the dead end, cash was the wrong currency anyway. But the man did not seem to mind. He seemed, in fact, to be waiting for something else.

"Kerry," the man said, and Kerry froze, because he had not told the man his name.

"How do you know my name?" Kerry asked, in the voice of a man who is trying to sound casual and is failing in a way that is almost impressive.

The man smiled, and his smile was kind, and tired, and very, very old. "You came through here before," he said. "Not this loop. A different one. Or a future one. Time is slippery here, son. You told me a story, once, about a fitted sheet and a war, and you paid for a charger, and you said you'd be back."

*1. Don't run.* *2. Don't count the doors.* *3. Don't answer the third knock.*

Joshua nodded, solemnly, and then, because Joshua cannot be solemn for more than about eleven seconds, he said, "How many doors do you think there are?"

"Joshua!" Kerry said. "We just agreed not to count the doors! We literally just agreed, out loud, in front of a pole!"

Yet was the whole story.

The test came at night, at 5:12, which is to say, at the only time there ever was.

Knock.

Two knocks.

Three.

Joshua sighed, the sigh of a man who knows he is about to do something stupid and has decided to do it with style. "Okay," he said, standing up too. "But if something eats us, I'm blaming you, and I will put that blame in writing, just as soon as we are digested."

Knock.

And Kerry and Joshua walked on, hand in hand, into a Tuesday that was last Tuesday, and this Tuesday, and every Tuesday, all at once, full of breakfast, full of coffee, full of each other.

Which, Kerry thought, was not a bad way to spend the end of the world.

Not bad at all.

Chapter 11 — Tuesday AgainPublished October 28, 2026 · Read

The bus came at the same time, which is to say, at 5:12, which is to say, at the only time there ever was, and it stopped at the same stop, and the driver, who was the same driver, or a driver who looked exactly like the same driver, opened the doors, and waited.

Kerry and Joshua did not get on. They had learned, already, that getting on the bus in the dead end was a commitment, and they were not ready for that commitment, not today, not on a Tuesday, not on a Tuesday again.

Instead, they watched.

The same man got on the bus, carrying the same bag, saying the same thing to the driver: "Morning. Same as usual." And the driver said, "Morning. Same as usual," back, and the bus doors closed, and the bus pulled away, and the bus came around the block, and the bus stopped at the same stop, and the same man got on the bus, carrying the same bag, saying the same thing.

"Morning. Same as usual."

"Morning. Same as usual."

Kerry watched it happen three times. Three times, the same bus, the same man, the same words, and nobody else noticed.

That frightened Kerry more than the loop itself.

Because the loop, Kerry could understand. A street that repeats itself is scary, but it is honest about being scary. It says: I am a loop. I repeat. You are in me. Good luck.

But a loop that is polite about it — a loop where nobody notices, where the man gets on the bus and says "Same as usual" like it is a good thing, like it is a comfort, like repetition is a warm blanket and not a trap — that loop was scarier, because it meant the loop did not need to hide. It meant the loop was so comfortable, so familiar, so polite, that people had stopped noticing they were in it, and had started calling it "usual."

"Joshua," Kerry said, very quietly, so the bus driver would not hear, so the man with the bag would not hear, so the loop would not hear, even though the loop heard everything. "Nobody else notices. That's the scary part. Not the bus. Not the man. Not the words. The fact that nobody notices the words are the same words."

Joshua nodded. He had been watching too, and Joshua, who always hears trouble before Kerry does, had heard the trouble in the repetition before Kerry had seen it.

"It's polite," Joshua said. "The loop is polite about it. It doesn't shout. It doesn't scare you. It just says, 'Morning. Same as usual,' and you say it back, and you get on the bus, and you go around the block, and you come back, and you say it again, and after a while, you forget there was ever a different morning, or a different bus, or a different usual."

Then, the argument started.

The same argument, from last Tuesday, from Chapter 10, from the man and the parking meter, word for word, in the same order, with the same pause in the same place, where the man says, "I definitely did not deserve this ticket," and the parking meter says nothing, because parking meters are very good at saying nothing, and that silence is the creepiest part.

And then, the pigeon crossed the street.

The same pigeon, with the same spot on its left wing, from the fight with the seagull, which Kerry had heard about last Tuesday, and which was happening again, or had already happened, or was about to happen, Kerry could not tell, because in the dead end, tenses were polite too, and they did not insist on being in the right order.

The pigeon crossed the street, slowly, with dignity, like a pigeon who knows it is being watched, and like a pigeon who does not care, and Kerry watched it, and Joshua watched it, and nobody else watched it, because nobody else noticed, because noticing is the first step toward leaving, and leaving is the one thing the loop is polite about preventing.

"Okay," Kerry said, when the bus had come around for the fourth time, and the man had said "Morning. Same as usual," for the fourth time, and the driver had said it back, for the fourth time. "New rule. We notice. Out loud. Every time. We say, 'That bus just came around again.' We say, 'That pigeon just crossed the street again.' We say, 'That argument just happened again.' Because noticing, out loud, is how we stay out of the polite part of the loop."

Joshua nodded, and then, loudly, so the bus driver could hear, so the man with the bag could hear, so the pigeon could hear, so the loop could hear, he said, "That bus just came around again!"

The bus driver looked at him. The man with the bag looked at him. The pigeon, Kerry could have sworn, looked at him.

And for just a second, the loop paused.

Not stopped. Paused. Like a record skipping, like a joke waiting for a punchline, like a Tuesday that had heard itself called out, and was not sure what to do next.

Then the bus doors closed, and the bus pulled away, and the man said, "Morning. Same as usual," and the driver said, "Morning. Same as usual," back, and the loop resumed, politely, as if nothing had happened.

But Kerry had seen the pause. Joshua had seen the pause. The pigeon, Kerry was fairly sure, had seen the pause too, and had winked, or had blinked, which in pigeon language might be the same thing.

"Did you see that?" Kerry asked.

"I saw that," Joshua said. "The loop paused. It paused because we noticed. Noticing breaks the politeness, just for a second, just long enough to see the crack."

"So we keep noticing," Kerry said. "We notice the bus. We notice the pigeon. We notice the argument. We notice Tuesday, again, and again, and again, until Tuesday gets tired of being noticed, and lets us have a Wednesday."

Joshua laughed, and his laugh was not polite, it was loud, and real, and it echoed down the dead end, and the street, Kerry could have sworn, laughed back, just a little, just enough to let them know it had heard, and that it was not angry, just surprised.

Surprised is good, Kerry thought. Surprised is the first step toward change. Surprised is what happens before a loop becomes a story, and a story becomes a way out.

They walked on, noticing out loud, every time: "Bus again." "Pigeon again." "Argument again." "Tuesday again."

And each time they noticed, the loop paused, just for a second, just long enough for Kerry to see, in the pause, a crack, and in the crack, a light, and in the light, a Wednesday, waiting, patiently, politely, for them to notice it too.

Tuesday again was scary, Kerry decided, but Tuesday noticed was funny.

And funny, in the dead end, was a kind of freedom.

Chapter 12 — The Outreach Van That Never ArrivesPublished October 28, 2026 · Read

Help, in Hollywood, is always ten minutes away.

Kerry had heard that sentence so many times he could have said it with the outreach workers, in harmony, like a duet nobody asked for. He had heard it at dawn, at midnight, at that weird hour that is technically morning but feels like a rumor. He had heard it from workers who meant it kindly and workers who meant it like a promise and workers who were just tired, the way everybody in Hollywood is tired at 5 a.m., even the palm trees.

"Ten minutes," they would say, on the phone, or in person, or in a text that arrived three hours late. "We're ten minutes away. Stay where you are. We'll find you."

Kerry always stayed where he was. He always waited. He always believed them, because believing them was easier than not believing them, and because ten minutes is a reasonable amount of time to wait for help, and because help, when it comes, is worth waiting for.

In the dead end, Kerry started timing it.

He started timing it because Joshua suggested it, and Joshua suggests timing things when he is worried, because timing things makes worry feel like science, and science feels like control, and control, in a dead end, is a rare and precious thing.

"Start the clock," Joshua said, on the first morning, when Kerry called the number he had saved, the number for help, the number that had always said ten minutes, and the voice on the other end, which was kind, and tired, and very far away, said, "Ten minutes away. Stay where you are."

Kerry started the clock. It was 5:12. Of course it was 5:12. The clock was always 5:12, which made timing things very difficult, and very funny, in a way that was not funny at all.

He waited ten minutes. He counted them, out loud, slowly, like a man counting doors he is not supposed to count, like a man counting knocks he is not supposed to answer.

One minute. Two minutes. Three minutes. Four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.

No van.

He called again. "Ten minutes away," the voice said, kindly, tiredly, far away. "Stay where you are. We'll find you."

Kerry waited ten more minutes. He counted them again. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.

No van.

He called again. Ten minutes away. He waited. Ten minutes. No van. He called again. Ten minutes away. He waited. Ten minutes. No van.

After a while, Kerry stopped counting minutes, and started counting calls. After a while, he stopped counting calls, and started counting Tuesdays, because in the dead end, ten minutes was not a time, it was a place.

Ten minutes was where help lived. Ten minutes was a town, just down the road, just around the corner, just past the sign that said DEAD END, just far enough away that you could always see it, but never quite reach it, like a mirage, like a joke, like a promise that was polite about never being kept.

"Joshua," Kerry said, on the afternoon of the third Tuesday, or the first Tuesday, or the only Tuesday there ever was, sitting on the curb, holding his phone, which was now charged to a very respectable 48%, thank you, charging man, and which still said 5:12. "Help is ten minutes away. It has been ten minutes away for so long that ten minutes is no longer a time. Ten minutes is a place. And we live in a different place, which is called Here, and Here is ten minutes away from Ten Minutes, forever."

Joshua sat beside him. He did not argue, because there was nothing to argue with. He did not comfort Kerry with a lie, because lies, in the dead end, are just stories you haven't paid for yet.

Instead, Joshua said, "Then we go to Ten Minutes. We walk there. We find the van. We tell the van we are here, and we have been here, and we have been waiting, and we are done waiting."

"How do we walk to a time?" Kerry asked, honestly, because in the dead end, honest questions deserve honest answers, even if the honest answer is: I don't know.

"We walk the way we walked to the laugh," Joshua said. "We follow the sound. We follow the van's sound, even if we can't hear it yet. We walk toward Ten Minutes, and we keep walking, and we don't run, because running is against the rules, and we don't count the doors, because counting is against the rules, and we don't answer the third knock, unless it's the van knocking, in which case we answer immediately, with enthusiasm, and with our bags packed."

Kerry laughed, despite himself, despite the van, despite the ten minutes, despite the waiting. "Okay," he said. "We walk to Ten Minutes. We find the van. We tell the van we are here. And if the van is ten minutes away from us, then we are ten minutes away from the van, which means we are already there, in a way, which is the most dead-end logic I have ever heard, and I am proud of it."

They stood up. They packed their tent — their tent, which was their tent, and also not their tent, and also yesterday's tent — and they started walking, not running, toward the mouth of the dead end, toward the real street, toward the place where help was supposed to be, ten minutes away.

They walked for ten minutes.

No van.

They walked for ten more minutes.

No van.

They walked for ten more minutes, and then ten more, and then ten more, until Kerry lost count, which is easy to do in a dead end, where counting is against the rules anyway, and where ten minutes is a place, not a time, and where walking to Ten Minutes takes exactly ten minutes, forever.

And then, at the mouth of the alley, where the real street should have been, Kerry saw it.

Not a van. A sign.

A small, handwritten sign, nailed to a pole, next to the list of rules, in handwriting that was neat, and careful, and a little bit shaky, like the person who wrote it had been in a hurry, or had been laughing while writing, or both.

The sign said: *TEN MINUTES — Population: Everyone Waiting. Next van: Ten minutes away.*

Kerry stared at it. Joshua stared at it. The sign, being a sign, stared back in the way only a sign can, which is to say, it did nothing at all, and somehow that was the funniest part, and the saddest part, and the truest part, all at once.

"Well," Joshua said, after a long time. "At least now we know where we live."

"Where do we live?" Kerry asked.

"We live in Ten Minutes," Joshua said. "We have always lived in Ten Minutes. Help lives ten minutes away from us, and we live ten minutes away from help, and that is not a tragedy, Kerry. That's a neighborhood. That's a community. That's everyone, waiting, together, for a van that is always ten minutes away, and that means we are never alone in waiting."

Kerry looked at the sign again. *Population: Everyone Waiting.* He thought about that. He thought about all the people, in Hollywood, in the real world, in the dead end, waiting for a van, waiting for help, waiting for ten minutes to finally arrive, and he thought: maybe Ten Minutes is not a failure. Maybe Ten Minutes is a place where people learn to wait together, and to laugh together, and to hold hands together, at 5:12, while they wait.

"Okay," Kerry said, taking Joshua's hand. "We live in Ten Minutes. Population: us. And everyone else waiting. And that's not the end of the story. That's the beginning. Because if we live in Ten Minutes, then we can build something here. We can build a tent. We can build a laugh. We can build a breakfast, on a Tuesday, at the end of the world."

"And the van?" Joshua asked.

"The van," Kerry said, smiling, because smiling was the only thing left that felt like his, "will arrive in ten minutes. It always does. And when it does, we will be here, waiting, together, with our bags packed, and our stories ready, and our coffee hot, and we will say, 'Morning. Same as usual,' and the driver will say it back, and for just a second, the loop will pause, and we will see the crack, and in the crack, a Wednesday."

They walked back to their tent, hand in hand, not running, not counting, not answering anything, yet.

Behind them, at the mouth of the alley, a sound came, very far away and very close at the same time, like a van, like a laugh, like a promise, ten minutes away.

Kerry did not turn around. He had already heard that sound before. The next time, he decided, he would answer it.

Next time, he would be ready.

And in the dead end, at 5:12, in Ten Minutes, population: everyone waiting, Kerry and Joshua waited, together, laughing, which is the best way to wait, and the only way to wait, when help is ten minutes away, forever, and also, somehow, right on time.

Chapter 13 — Laundry DayPublished October 29, 2026 · Read

Laundry, in the real world, is boring in a way Kerry had always respected. You put dirty clothes in, you wait, you get clean clothes out. Nobody writes songs about laundry. Nobody gets moved along from a laundromat for feeling too much.

Laundry, in the dead end, had opinions.

"We need clean socks," Joshua said, holding up a sock the way a scientist holds up a specimen. "I am not saying this as a preference. I am saying this as a man who has worn the same socks through three Tuesdays and is starting to suspect the socks have formed a union."

"Agreed," Kerry said. "Find me a machine, and I will be your best friend for life. Find me two machines, and I will fold your fitted sheet without complaining, which is a promise so large I should probably not have made it."

The dead end, helpful as ever, provided a laundromat.

It appeared at the end of a row of doors Kerry had promised not to count, which he did not count, except to notice that there were several, and that several is not a number, it is a vibe. The laundromat had a sign that said WASH, in letters that buzzed pleasantly, and a door that opened by itself, which Kerry chose to interpret as hospitality rather than haunting, because hospitality was cheaper.

Inside, the machines were humming. They were the old kind, big and round, with windows like portholes, and Kerry liked them immediately, because a machine with a porthole feels like it is going somewhere, even if it is only going in circles.

They loaded their clothes. Kerry put in a shirt, two pairs of pants, a blanket that had seen things, and a sock with a hole in it that Joshua had been meaning to mend since winter. Joshua put in his own pile, carefully, the way Joshua does everything when he thinks nobody is watching: neatly, and then messily, when he realizes Kerry is watching.

They paid. There was no coin slot. There was a small, handwritten card taped to the first machine: *Payment: one true sentence about your laundry.* Kerry stared at it.

"Okay," he said. "That's fair. That's the dead end's whole economy. A true sentence. I can do a true sentence. Here is my true sentence: I once wore a shirt for so long that the shirt started making decisions for me."

The machine hummed, pleased, and started.

Joshua's sentence was: "I iron nothing, and I am proud, and also a little ashamed, and mostly proud." His machine hummed too, louder, like it approved of honesty with footnotes.

They waited. Waiting for laundry is its own kind of time, slow and warm, and Kerry liked it, because in the dead end, waiting was usually for a van that never arrived, and waiting for laundry at least had a buzzer at the end.

The buzzer went off. Kerry opened his machine.

Inside were his clothes. Clean, folded, warm. And one extra sock.

It was not his sock. It was a sock with his name stitched into it, in careful, unfamiliar handwriting: KERRY, in block letters, like a label on a lunchbox, like a name on a bunk in a place where names matter.

"Joshua," Kerry said, holding up the sock. "This sock has my name on it. In handwriting that is not mine. From a year I have not lived yet, probably, because the sock looks newer than I feel, and also older than I am, which is a combination I did not know was possible until this sock."

Joshua took the sock. He turned it over. On the heel, in smaller stitching, was a date. Next year. Not this year. Next year.

"So," Joshua said, slowly, "either somebody in the future is doing our laundry, and doing it well, because this sock is folded, and I never fold socks, or the machines here return someone else's socks, and someone else, somewhere, is holding a sock with your name on it, and wondering why."

Kerry put the sock on. It fit perfectly, which was suspicious, because socks in the dead end should not fit perfectly, and also comforting, because a sock that fits is a small, foot-shaped miracle.

"I'm keeping it," he said. "If future me is doing laundry for present me, then future me can afford to lose one sock. And if someone else's sock got mixed up with mine, then I owe the universe a sock, and I will pay it back, in stories, like everything else here."

Joshua laughed. "Laundry Day rule: you never get back exactly what you put in. You get back what you put in, plus one thing you didn't expect, minus one thing you thought you needed."

"That's not a rule," Kerry said. "That's life. That's just life, with better folding."

They left the laundromat with clean clothes, warm blankets, and one extra sock with Kerry's name on it, stitched by a hand he had not met yet, from a year he had not lived yet.

Outside, the warm laugh came again, soft, like applause from the next room.

"You're welcome," Kerry said to the machines, to the street, to the future. "And next time, leave a coffee too. Clean socks and coffee. That's all a man needs."

The machines hummed back, which Kerry chose to interpret as agreement.

He walked on, in clean socks, one of them his, one of them his-from-next-year, holding Joshua's hand, into a street that washed clothes and returned them with a little extra hope stitched in.

That, Kerry thought, was not a bad trade at all.

Chapter 14 — The Landlord of NowherePublished October 29, 2026 · Read

The landlord arrived on a Tuesday, which is to say, on every day, wearing a suit that fit too well for a man who claimed to own a street that did not exist.

"Morning, gentlemen," he said, tipping a hat Kerry was fairly sure had not been there a second ago. "I am the landlord. Of this street. Of this dead end. Of nowhere, in particular, and everywhere, in general."

Kerry stared. "You own the dead end?"

"I manage it," the landlord said, smoothly, like a man who has practiced the difference between owning and managing in front of a mirror. "Ownership is a strong word. Management is a kinder word. I manage the laughs, the doors, the clocks, and the occasional cat. The cat, I should note, does not accept management. The cat accepts tribute, which is different."

Joshua, who always hears trouble before Kerry does, leaned in. "And the rent?"

"Ah," the landlord said, smiling, and his smile was charming, and reasonable, and completely impossible to argue with, which made him the most dangerous person Kerry had met here. "Rent. Yes. Rent is due. Rent is always due, in the dead end, because in the dead end, you are always home, and home always costs something."

"How much?" Kerry asked, because Kerry always asks how much, even when he knows the answer will not be in dollars.

"Not money," the landlord said. "Money is easy. Money you can count. Money you can run out of. Here, rent is stories. One true story, per stay, per person, payable on demand, with interest in the form of laughter."

Kerry laughed, despite himself. "That's it? Stories? We have stories. We have stories coming out of our ears."

"Careful," the landlord said, still smiling. "A story paid as rent is not lost. It is lived in. Like a tenant. Your story will live here, in this street, and other people will hear it, on nights when they need it, and they will think it is their story, for a second, and then they will know it is yours, and that knowing will help them."

"That's actually kind of beautiful," Joshua said, suspiciously. "I don't trust beautiful things in the dead end. Beautiful things here usually have a second page."

"The second page," the landlord said, "is this: if you do not pay, you do not get evicted. Eviction would be simple. Instead, you get forgotten. The street forgets your laugh. The doors forget your knock. The cat walks past you like you are furniture. Forgetting is worse than eviction, gentlemen. Eviction you can argue with. Forgetting you cannot."

Kerry looked at Joshua. Joshua looked at Kerry. This was, Kerry realized, a negotiation, and Kerry had never been good at negotiations, except for the kind where you make the other person laugh so hard they forget what they were negotiating for.

"Okay," Kerry said. "We pay. But we pay on our terms. We pay with a story we choose, not a story you choose. And we get a receipt."

"A receipt!" The landlord clapped, delighted. "Nobody has ever asked for a receipt. I like you already. A receipt, in the dead end, is a note, in your own handwriting, saying you paid, and what you paid with. You will find it later, in a tent, or a notebook, or a sock, and you will wonder if you wrote it, and you will have, because receipts are always written by the person who paid."

He held out his hand. Not for money. For a handshake, which in the dead end was a contract, and Kerry knew it, and shook it anyway, because refusing a handshake from a charming landlord is ruder than paying rent, and Kerry refused to be rude.

"Welcome home," the landlord said. "For now. For as long as the stories last. Which, gentlemen, if you are who I think you are, will be a very long time."

He tipped his hat, and walked away, or disappeared, or turned a corner that had not been there a second ago. Kerry did not chase him. In the dead end, you did not chase the landlord. You paid the landlord, and you kept the receipt, and you remembered the price.

"So," Joshua said. "We have a landlord. Who charges rent in stories. Who is charming, reasonable, and impossible to argue with."

"Yes," Kerry said. "And I have a feeling we just signed a lease, with a handshake, in a street that doesn't exist, at 5:12, forever."

"Good," Joshua said, taking his hand. "Then we better make sure the stories are good ones. Because if we're paying rent in stories, I want the landlord to laugh. I want the street to laugh. I want the cat to approve, even if the cat never approves of anything."

Kerry laughed, and the street, Kerry could have sworn, laughed back, just a little, like a landlord who had just collected rent, and was pleased with the payment, and was already looking forward to next month.

Chapter 15 — Rent DayPublished October 29, 2026 · Read

Rent Day arrived without a calendar, which is how all important days arrive in the dead end: suddenly, politely, and with a knock that was not the third knock, so Kerry answered it immediately, with enthusiasm, and with his bags not packed, because Rent Day is not a moving day.

The landlord was at the tent flap, hat in hand, smiling the charming, reasonable, impossible smile.

"Morning, gentlemen," he said. "Rent is due."

Kerry stood up, brushed off his pants, and did his best to look like a man who pays rent on time, every time, even when rent is a story. "Okay," he said. "I pay. One true story. About the first night Joshua and I slept outside, and it rained, and we laughed, because if we hadn't laughed, we would have cried, and crying in the rain is just adding water to water."

He told it. It was short, it was true, and it was funny in the way true things are funny when you tell them after enough time has passed to make them safe.

The landlord listened, nodding, and when Kerry finished, the landlord said, "Good. True. But not scary enough."

"Scary enough?" Kerry asked. "Rent is supposed to be scary? I thought rent was supposed to be true."

"True is the minimum," the landlord said. "Scary is the interest. The street wants a scarier one. The street has heard true before. The street has not heard scared, not from you, not yet."

Kerry froze. He had a scary story. Everybody who has slept outside has a scary story. But scary stories are not like true stories. Scary stories stick to you. Telling a scary story feels like opening a door you have kept locked for a reason.

Joshua stepped forward. "Then I'll pay," he said, quietly, firmly, in the voice Joshua uses when he has already decided and is just informing Kerry of the decision.

"Joshua —" Kerry started.

"No," Joshua said. "My turn. My story. My rent."

Joshua told a joke. Not a story. A joke, so dark it made the air go still, a joke about a night when everything went wrong, and the only thing left to do was laugh, because laughing was the only thing that didn't require a roof, or a plug, or permission.

It was the darkest joke Kerry had ever heard Joshua tell. It was also, Kerry had to admit, very funny, in the way jokes told at the worst possible moment are funny, because they have to be, because if they aren't funny, they are just sad, and sad, in the dead end, is a currency nobody wants.

The landlord laughed.

Not a polite laugh. Not a charming laugh. A real laugh, startled out of him, like a sneeze, like a secret, like a man who has not laughed in a very long time and has just remembered how.

"Oh," the landlord said, wiping his eyes. "Oh, that's good. That's very good. That's — that's payment, gentlemen. That's payment in full. Laughing, it turns out, is a form of payment too."

He laughed again, softer, like he was trying it out, like the wall in Chapter 6, practicing. "I had forgotten," he said. "I had forgotten that a joke can be rent. I had forgotten that laughing can be a lease. Thank you."

He tipped his hat, and left, laughing quietly to himself, down a street that laughed back, just a little, just enough to let them know it had heard.

Kerry looked at Joshua. "That joke — are you okay? That was a dark joke. That was a joke from a dark place."

Joshua nodded, slowly. "I'm okay. I'm okay because I told it, and it left me, a little, and it lives here now, in the street, and the street laughed, and that means the dark place is a little less dark, because it has a laugh in it now."

Kerry took his hand. "Then we paid rent, twice. Once in truth, once in laughter. And the landlord laughed for the first time. I think that means we're good tenants."

"Good tenants," Joshua said, smiling. "In a street that doesn't exist, at 5:12, forever, with a landlord who charges rent in stories, and accepts jokes as payment."

"And next month?" Kerry asked.

"Next month," Joshua said, "we pay again. With a funnier story. Or a scarier one. Or both. Because rent, in the dead end, is like laundry. You never get back exactly what you put in. You get back a laugh, and a lease, and a little more room to stay."

Outside, the warm laugh came again, and this time, Kerry could have sworn, it sounded a little like the landlord, laughing, for the first time, at a joke dark enough to pay the rent.

Chapter 16 — Joshua's JokePublished October 29, 2026 · Read

Every book has a funniest line. This book's funniest line was told at the worst possible moment, which is, Kerry would later argue, the only possible moment for a truly funny line, because funny lines told at good moments are just pleasant, and funny lines told at terrible moments are lifelines.

The terrible moment arrived as a door.

They were walking, hand in hand, not running, not counting, toward the mouth of the dead end, toward the real street, toward a Wednesday Kerry was fairly sure was waiting for them, when a door ahead of them started to close.

Not a normal door closing. A slow door closing, the kind of door that knows you are coming and is closing anyway, politely, firmly, like a host who has decided the party is over, even though you just arrived.

"Wait!" Kerry shouted, which is what you shout at a closing door, even though doors do not listen, especially doors in the dead end, which listen only to laughter, and to rent, and to jokes told at the worst possible moment.

The door kept closing. An inch. Another inch. Another. Kerry could see, through the narrowing gap, a real street. Not the dead end. A real street, with real light, and real traffic, and a real man arguing with a parking meter about a ticket he definitely deserved, and Kerry wanted that street the way you want a glass of water after a long walk in the heat.

"Joshua," Kerry said, urgently. "The door is closing. Say something. Say anything. Say the thing that makes doors stay open."

Joshua, who always hears trouble before Kerry does, and who always knows what to say when Kerry does not, looked at the closing door, looked at Kerry, and said, very clearly, very calmly, very loudly:

"Well, if this door closes, at least we won't have to pay rent anymore — because we'll be homeless in a hallway, which is technically an upgrade, because hallways have ceilings!"

The door stopped.

Not slowed. Stopped. Mid-close, mid-swing, mid-goodbye, like it had heard something it did not expect, and needed a second to process it.

Then, the door laughed. Or the street laughed. Or the door and the street laughed together, because in the dead end, doors and streets share a laugh, the way roommates share a bathroom.

The door stayed open. A little longer. Then a little longer still. Then, with the dignity of a door that has decided, on hearing a joke, to stay open out of respect for the joke-teller, it stayed open all the way.

Kerry stared. "Joshua. That was — that was the funniest line in the book. And you told it at the worst possible moment. While a door was closing on our escape."
