Chapter 51 — The Second Move-AlongPublished October 29, 2026 · Read

Back in real Hollywood, Kerry expected everything to feel different. It did not. It felt exactly the same, only louder, which was Hollywood's way of saying welcome back, we missed you, now please move.

They had found a curb. A good curb, as curbs go. Not too slanted, not too close to a bus stop, not too far from a light that actually worked. Joshua had just gotten the tent poles to cooperate — a rare diplomatic achievement — when the flashlight came on.

"Sir, you gotta move along. You can't stay here."

Kerry laughed before he could stop himself. It burst out of him, honest and loud and completely inappropriate for a man being told to move at dawn, and the cop blinked, because cops do not usually get laughed at by the people they are moving along, at least not in a friendly way.

"I'm sorry," Kerry said, holding up a hand. "I'm sorry. It's not you. It's the speech. I've heard that speech so many times, and hearing it out here, on a real street, with real traffic behind you — it sounds like a cover version."

"A cover version of what?" the cop asked. He was younger than the dead-end cop. Different face, different voice, same tired patience in his shoulders.

"Of a song I know," Kerry said. "A song I have heard in a place that does not exist, sung by a man who may not exist either, at a time that definitely does not exist."

Joshua, who was folding the tent with the speed of a man who has done this while being watched before, said, "He means we will move. We are moving. Look at us, moving. This is us, moving, with enthusiasm and grace."

"We are moving," Kerry agreed. "We are the most obedient people you will move along all week. Possibly all year. You should put that in your report."

The cop almost smiled. Almost is a powerful word in Hollywood. Almost smiled, almost stayed, almost understood — Kerry had lived his whole life on almosts, and he recognized this one for what it was: a man doing a job he did not invent, talking to men who did not invent their situation either.

"Where do you want us to go?" Kerry asked, and he meant it, not as a joke this time, or not only as a joke. "Because out here, somebody always tells us to move, and nobody ever tells us where to. Is there a place? Is there a list? I would love a list. A brochure, even. 'Welcome to Hollywood: Places You Are Allowed to Exist.' I asked for one before. I am still waiting."

The cop looked down the street, then back at them. "I don't have a list," he said. "I just have this block, tonight."

"Fair enough," Kerry said. "Tonight, this block is yours. Tomorrow night, it will be somebody else's block, and we will be somebody else's problem. That is the system. I am not blaming you for the system. I am just noting, for the record, that the system is weird."

They moved. That is what you do. You move, you find a new spot, you tell yourself this spot is better, quieter, safer, and then at some hour that is not a real hour, somebody tells you to move again. Only this time, as they walked, Kerry kept laughing, quietly, to himself, because the second move-along had taught him something the first one never could: the speech was not magic. It was a job. And a job could be done kindly, or tiredly, or badly, but it was still just a job. The street that laughed, on the other hand — that street had never been just a job. It had been a host. A strange host, a host with rules and jokes and a cat, but a host.

"Why are you still laughing?" Joshua asked, as they turned a corner that was not a dead end, just a regular corner, with a regular sign, and regular traffic that did not stop for them at all.

"Because," Kerry said, "out here, the speech ends. In there, it never ends. And I think I prefer a speech that ends, even if I have to hear it again tomorrow."

"That's a low bar," Joshua said.

"It's my bar," Kerry said. "I set it myself. It is low, it is sturdy, and I can step over it without help."

They found another curb. Not as good. Good enough. Joshua unfolded the tent again, slower this time, because nobody was watching with a flashlight, and slowness is a luxury you only notice when it is gone.

Kerry sat down beside him and looked back the way they had come. No sign. No laugh. No clock stuck at 5:12. Just Hollywood, humming, arguing with its parking meters, being itself.

"I miss it a little," Kerry admitted.

"I know," Joshua said. "Me too. Which is ridiculous."

"Completely ridiculous," Kerry said. "And completely true. Both at once. That's our specialty now."

They slept, or tried to, in the way you sleep when you know you might have to move again, which is to say, lightly, and with one ear open. Somewhere in the night, far away and very close at the same time, Kerry thought he heard a laugh. Warm. Familiar. Not mocking. Practicing, maybe. Waiting, definitely.

He did not get up to chase it. He had learned that much, at least. Some laughs you walk toward. Some laughs you let come to you. This one, he suspected, would find him again soon enough, whether he chased it or not.

In the morning, the pigeon was there. It looked at him. He looked at it. Neither of them said anything, which was probably for the best, because if the pigeon had started talking, Kerry would have had to revise a great many of his opinions about birds, and he was not ready for that before coffee.

"Morning," he said to the pigeon, because manners cost nothing, even when you have nothing.

The pigeon, Kerry would swear later, winked. Probably.

Chapter 52 — The Cop's NamePublished October 29, 2026 · Read

Kerry had never asked the dead-end cop his name. It had never occurred to him, which is strange, because Kerry asks everybody their name. He asks baristas, bus drivers, outreach workers, strangers on corners. Names are how you prove a person is real. And the cop, for all his politeness and his clipboard and his scar, had remained, in Kerry's mind, simply The Cop, capital T, capital C, like a job title that had eaten a man.

So the next time they were back in the dead end — and they were back, because everyone returns, eventually, and because Joshua had left a sock there, which is as good a reason as any — Kerry decided to ask.

"Can I ask you something?" Kerry said, when the flashlight clicked on at the mouth of the alley, right on schedule, at a time that was almost certainly 5:12.

"Sir," the cop said, "you gotta move along. You can't stay here."

"I know," Kerry said. "I know the speech. I could say it with you. In harmony. Like a duet nobody asked for. But before we do the speech, can I ask your name?"

The cop paused. Cops in the loop rarely pause. Pausing is not in the script. The flashlight dipped, just a little, and for a second Kerry saw not a uniform but a man, tired in the particular way of people who work nights and never quite catch up on sleep.

"I've had many," the cop said finally.

"Many names?" Joshua asked.

"Many," the cop said. "This job — it gives you a new one every few years, whether you want it or not. People call you what they need to call you. Officer. Sir. Hey. You. Man. Sometimes they don't call you anything at all. They just move."

Kerry thought about that. He thought about all the names he had been called, on the street and off it, kind ones and unkind ones, and how a name, given by someone else, could feel like a coat that did not fit, and how a name you chose for yourself could feel like a door you could actually walk through.

"Then let me give you one," Kerry said, before his brain could approve the idea, which was how most of his best and worst ideas arrived. "A good one. A name that fits. Not Officer. Not Hey. A name."

The cop looked at him for a long moment. "That's a terrible gift," he said. "And a generous one. Are you sure?"

"I'm sure," Kerry said. "Everybody deserves a name that is not just their job. Even — especially — a man whose job is telling other people to move."

Joshua, who could always tell when Kerry was about to do something sentimental and irreversible, put a hand on his arm. "Kerry. Think. If you name him, he becomes real. Real things can leave. Real things can be lost."

"Real things can also stay," Kerry said.

He thought. He thought about the cop's tired laugh, and the way his flashlight dipped when he was tired of holding it up, and the way he had once, in the middle of a move-along, called Kerry "son," and how that word had landed somewhere older than the alley.

"Eli," Kerry said. "Your name is Eli."

The cop — Eli — repeated it slowly, like tasting a word he had not tasted in years. "Eli," he said. "Eli. I like that. It sounds like somebody who goes home at the end of a shift. Somebody who has a chair that is his. Somebody who is not just a speech."

"Then be Eli," Kerry said. "Off duty, on duty, whenever you want. The speech can stay a speech. You don't have to be."

Eli laughed. Not the tired laugh. Not the warm laugh from the end of the street, either. A new laugh, small and surprised, like a man who had found a dollar in a coat he thought was empty.

"Eli," he said again, and clicked the flashlight off, and for a second the alley was dark, and then the streetlight came on, steady and warm, like a porch light left on for somebody coming home late.

"Well," Eli said, "Eli still has to tell you to move along. That's the job. But Eli can tell you nicely. And Eli can tell you where, this time. There's a spot two streets over, behind the bakery. Nobody moves you from behind the bakery before seven. The smell helps. It makes the whole thing feel less like a move-along and more like a morning."

Kerry stared. "You never told us where before."

"I never had a name before," Eli said simply. "Names change the job. That's why they take them away, sometimes. Or why we give them away ourselves, to make the job easier. But you gave one back. So now I owe you a where."

They went to the bakery spot. It was good. The smell was, indeed, helpful. And all night, Kerry thought about the terrible and generous gift of a name, and how giving someone a name did not make them yours, and did not make them stay, but did make them real enough to be thanked.

In the morning, Joshua said, "Eli. I like it. It fits him."

"I know," Kerry said. "I picked it. I have excellent taste in names. I named a cat once, and the cat respected me for a full week afterward, which is a record."

Joshua laughed. "You did not name the cat. The cat named itself. We just agreed."

"Same thing," Kerry said. "Agreement is the whole point."

And somewhere, at the mouth of a street that did not exist, a flashlight clicked on, and a voice that was no longer only a speech said, politely, and by name, "Sir. You gotta move along."

It sounded, Kerry thought, almost like a greeting.

There is a man in the dead end who claims to understand the clock. He is not the landlord, not the vendor, not Eli. Kerry looked down at his feet. "I'm standing on concrete."

"Yes," the man said, pleased, as if Kerry had proved his point. "Concrete at 5:12. Which is hinge-concrete. Very different from regular concrete. Regular concrete just sits there. Hinge-concrete holds the door open between yesterday and tomorrow."

"Okay," Kerry said. "So how do we get off the hinge?"

"You don't," the man said. "You learn to live on it. You put a chair on it. You have coffee on it. You tell jokes on it. Eventually the hinge becomes a porch. And a porch is a fine place to live, if you don't mind the door swinging."

Joshua frowned. "But outside, time moves. We left, and it was later. We came back, and it was 5:12 again. How does that work?"

"Ah," the man said, flipping pages. "Outside time is a river. Inside time is a puddle. A puddle that looks like a river if you stare at it long enough. You stepped out of the river into the puddle, and the puddle said, 'Welcome, stay a while, it is always 5:12 here, the water is fine.'"

"That is the worst explanation I have ever heard," Kerry said admiringly. "It explains nothing, and yet I feel like I understand less, which, according to you, might be the point."

"Exactly," the man said. "Some clocks are not for telling time. Some clocks are for telling you that time is not the boss of you. 5:12 is a clock that quit its job and became a landmark. Kerry thought about all the times he had waited — for a van that was ten minutes away, for help that was coming soon, for a morning that would finally be different — and how waiting had always felt like being stuck, and how 5:12, explained badly, suddenly felt less like being stuck and more like being early to something.

"So we're not stuck," Kerry said slowly. "We're early."

"Very early," the man said. "Years early, possibly. Or minutes early. In a puddle, it is hard to tell. That is the beauty of it. And the horror. Mostly the beauty, if you bring coffee."

"Do you have coffee?" Joshua asked hopefully.

"No," the man said. "I have explanations. Explanations are not coffee, but they are warm, in a way, if you hold them close."

They left the man to his notebook, and walked the loop, and Joshua's phone said 5:12, and Kerry's phone, which had charged to 3% in real Hollywood, said 5:12 too, which was either a coincidence or a conspiracy, and Kerry decided, on balance, to call it a landmark.

"Meet me at 5:12," Joshua said, taking his hand.

"I'm already here," Kerry said. "I never left. That's the joke. That's always been the joke."

And the street laughed, warmly, like it had heard a good explanation, badly told, and had decided to keep it anyway, because some explanations are not for understanding. They are for company, on a hinge, at a time that is also a place, where two men are standing, holding hands, early for everything, and exactly on time.

"Here," Kerry said.

Joshua, half asleep, said, "Good. Let nothing happen. Nothing is underrated."

"Did we sleep through the night?" Joshua asked, sitting up, hair wild, eyes hopeful.

"We slept through the night," Kerry said. "All of it. No move-along. No loop. No laugh. Just sleep."

"That's a miracle," Joshua said.

"That's a Tuesday," Kerry said, and then laughed, because Tuesday had once been a joke about a day that would not end, and now Tuesday was a miracle about a night that did, peacefully, on its own.

They packed the tent slowly. No rush. No performance pressure. No man with a clipboard watching them fold. Joshua folded it in three minutes instead of two, which felt decadent, like ordering dessert when you are already full.

"Do you think the loop let us go?" Joshua asked, as they walked away from the spot that was a spot again.

"I think the loop gave us a night off," Kerry said. "Like a host who says, 'Take the night, you look tired, the jokes will keep.' And I think we should accept it gracefully, and not ask too many questions, because questions are how you end up back on the hinge."

"Agreed," Joshua said. "No questions. Just coffee. Real coffee, if we can find it. And if we can't, pretend coffee, which is just hot water and hope, and hope, in Hollywood, is a renewable resource, if you know where to look."

Chapter 91 — The Clock, BilingualPublished October 29, 2026 · Read

The clock on the wall had never lied to Kerry. That was the strange part. It had never told the truth either, not exactly. It had simply said 5:12, over and over, with the confidence of a man who has said the same thing at every meeting for thirty years and has no plans to stop now.

Kerry stared at it that morning, the way you stare at a puzzle you have been carrying around in your pocket so long the edges have gone soft.

"Joshua," he said. "I think the clock is bilingual."

Joshua did not look up from folding the blanket. "Bilingual," he repeated, in the tone of a man who has learned that Kerry's sentences sometimes need a moment to finish arriving. "In what two languages?"

"5:12," Kerry said, "and every other time at once."

Joshua laughed, which was, Kerry thought, exactly the right response, and also exactly the wrong one, because the clock did not laugh back, and clocks that do not laugh back are usually serious about something.

"No, listen," Kerry said. "A joke has a setup, and a pause, and a punchline. This clock has a setup — 5:12, stuck, same as always — and it has a pause, which is all the time we spend waiting for it to move. And the punchline is always now. Right now. Not later. Not yesterday. Now. The clock is not broken. It is telling a joke, and the joke is that the time is always now, and we keep waiting for a different time to show up and rescue us."

Joshua sat down beside him. The one-eyed cat, who had been supervising from the curb, blinked its one good eye in a way that could have been agreement or could have been a cat being a cat, which is usually the same thing.

"So 5:12 means now," Joshua said.

"5:12 means now," Kerry said. "And also, underneath it, in smaller letters, in the language nobody reads unless they are really paying attention, it means every other time too. Morning coffee time. Midnight time. The time you were born, the time you laughed hardest, the time you finally got a good night's sleep. All of it, stacked up under 5:12 like a pile of laundry you keep meaning to fold."

Kerry put his hand on the wall, under the clock, the way he had once put his hand on a laughing wall, because in the dead end, touching things was how you asked them questions politely.

"Is that right?" he asked the clock. "Are you bilingual?"

The clock did not answer, because clocks do not answer, except that this one did, in its own way: the hands trembled, just a little, like a man trying not to laugh at his own joke before he gets to the punchline.

And then Kerry understood it, the way you understand a joke a second before everybody else laughs, which is the loneliest and best second there is.

The clock was not stuck. The clock was waiting. It was waiting for Kerry to read it correctly. Setup, pause, punchline. 5:12, waiting, now.

"Now," Kerry said out loud, testing it. "Now, now, now."

Joshua took his hand. "Now is a good time," he said. "Now is, historically, our best time. We have done our best work in now. We have held hands in now. We have laughed in now. Later has never done anything for us that now hasn't done better."

"Later is a rumor," Kerry said. "Like coffee before we found coffee. Like help being ten minutes away. Later is outreach time. Now is the only time that ever actually shows up."

The clock, Kerry could have sworn, ticked once. Just once. Not forward to 5:13 — that would have been too much, too soon, and the dead end never gave you too much too soon — but a tick, a small, polite tick, like a man clearing his throat before he speaks a second language.

Kerry wrote it down in his notebook, because the cart man had said everybody needs a notebook, and Kerry was starting to think the notebook was the only honest clock he owned.

*The clock speaks two languages: 5:12, and now. Learn both.*

Joshua read it over his shoulder. "That's a good rule," he said. "Better than don't run. Less scary. More useful."

"All the best rules are bilingual," Kerry said. "They mean one thing on the wall, and another thing in your chest."

They sat under the clock for a while, doing nothing, which in the dead end is never nothing, because doing nothing under a clock that says 5:12 is a kind of practice. Practice for now. Practice for reading jokes correctly. Practice for the day when the clock finally speaks its second language out loud, and everybody hears it, and everybody laughs, because the punchline was always now, and now has finally arrived.

The warm laugh came from the end of the street, soft, like applause from the next room, like a teacher who is pleased that a student has finally gotten the lesson.

Kerry laughed back, because that is what you do when you are scared and you don't want anybody, including yourself, to know it, and also because that is what you do when you finally get a joke, and the joke is good, and the joke is you, and the joke is now.

"Okay," he said, standing up, holding Joshua's hand, which was still in his, which was the real miracle here. "Let's go be bilingual. Let's go speak now, fluently, for the rest of the day."

"And tomorrow?" Joshua asked.

"Tomorrow," Kerry said, "is just now, wearing a different hat. We'll recognize it when it shows up."

They walked on, under a clock that said 5:12, in a street that said dead end, at a time that said now, in two languages, both of which Kerry was finally learning to read.

Chapter 92 — Now, PracticedPublished October 29, 2026 · Read

Practicing now turned out to be harder than planning an escape.

Planning an escape was easy. You could do it in the future tense, which is the tense of people who are not actually doing anything. "We will leave. We will find a door. We will be free." The future tense is a wonderful place to live, because nothing in it ever has to happen. You can furnish it beautifully and never pay rent.

Now was different. Now wanted rent, in cash, immediately, in the form of small, funny, brave choices.

Kerry's first now-choice of the day was embarrassingly small. He chose to drink his coffee while it was hot, instead of saving it for later, instead of carrying it around like a treasure, instead of telling himself he would enjoy it more when things were better.

"Revolutionary," Joshua said, watching him sip. "Truly. Historians will mark this day."

"Shut up," Kerry said, happily. "This is practice. This is me, escaping, in the present tense."

His second now-choice was to tell the truth to a stranger, quickly, before he could dress it up. The stranger was a woman who had just arrived in the loop, blinking, holding a bag, looking the way Kerry had looked on the first morning: like a man who had been moved along so many times he had started to move along preemptively, just to save time.

"Is this a bad place?" she asked Kerry, in a whisper, like she was afraid the street would hear her being rude about it.

"No," Kerry said, before he could plan a better answer. "It's a strange place. It's a funny place. It's a place that will teach you things you didn't ask to learn, and then it will give you coffee, and then it will take your story as rent, and you will be annoyed, and then you will be grateful, and both of those will be true at the same time."

She stared at him. "That's a lot for a first answer."

"That's now," Kerry said. "Now is a lot. Future answers are neater. Now answers are true."

His third now-choice was the bravest, which is to say, the smallest. He chose not to run from the laugh. For months — or days, or loops, time being bilingual and unhelpful — Kerry had walked toward the laugh while also, secretly, flinching from it, the way you walk toward a dog you are not sure is friendly. Today he walked toward it without flinching, and the laugh, startled, sounded surprised, and then pleased, like a host whose guest has finally stopped hovering in the doorway and come all the way inside.

"See?" Joshua said, catching up, holding his hand. "That's escaping. That's not planning an escape. That's escaping, one choice at a time, while your feet are still on the ground."

"My feet have never left the ground," Kerry said. "My plans have. My plans have been orbiting the dead end like a satellite, taking pictures, writing reports, never landing."

"Land them," Joshua said. "Land one plan a day. Today's plan is coffee, hot. Tomorrow's plan is whatever now decides tomorrow is."

They practiced now all afternoon, which is to say, they did ordinary things with extraordinary attention. They folded the blanket, slowly, instead of in a hurry. They ate, slowly, instead of while walking. They listened to the one-eyed cat purr, which is a sound the cat makes only when it approves of you, and the cat had approved of them for a while now, but today Kerry actually heard it, instead of hearing it later, in memory, which is where he usually heard good things, after they were already over.

At one point, the polite cop appeared at the mouth of the alley, flashlight in hand, clipboard under his arm, ready, Kerry was sure, to deliver the speech.

"Sir," the cop began, polite as ever. "You gotta move along. You can't stay —"

"Now," Kerry said, interrupting him, gently, the way you interrupt a song you already know the words to, not to be rude, but because you love it and you want to sing along. "We are staying, now. Not forever. Not later. Now. Now we are staying, and now we are moving, because moving and staying are both now, if you do them on purpose."

The cop looked at him for a long moment. Then he did something cops are not supposed to do in the middle of a move-along. He nodded, slowly, like a man who has heard a new version of an old speech and is considering it.

"Now," the cop said, testing the word. "Now is a good time."

"It is the only time," Kerry said.

The cop clicked his flashlight off, which in the dead end is practically a standing ovation, and walked away, or disappeared, or turned a corner that had not been there a second ago. Kerry did not chase him. In the dead end, you do not chase the help. You thank the help, and you keep the now, and you practice it again tomorrow.

That night, Kerry wrote in his notebook: *Escape is not a future event. Escape is a present-tense verb. Conjugate it daily.*

Joshua read it and said, "You are conjugating beautifully."

"I am conjugating," Kerry said, "one small, funny, brave choice at a time, which is the only conjugation that has ever worked for me."

They fell asleep holding hands, in a tent that was theirs and also yesterday's, in a street that was a dead end and also a beginning, at a time that was 5:12 and also now.

And now, Kerry thought, just before sleep took him, was finally a tense he could live in.

Chapter 93 — The Choice, SmallPublished October 29, 2026 · Read

The small choice was coffee. That was all. It was not a door, or a key, or a dramatic exit, or a speech. It was coffee, with a woman who had been in the loop since 1998 and still made coffee like it was a normal morning, which, in the loop, is the most radical thing a person can do.

Kerry had met her before, in the other tents, in the chapter of his life where other people's tents were folded neatly and labeled with years. She had a tent, and a kettle, and a patience that made Kerry feel like a man who had just discovered patience was a skill, not a gift.

"Stay for coffee?" she asked, on a morning that was 5:12, like every morning, and also, somehow, different, because Kerry had practiced now all week, and now had started to taste different, like a coffee you finally drink while it is hot.

Kerry's first instinct was to say no, politely, quickly, the way you say no when you are in a hurry to get somewhere, even if you are not sure where somewhere is. His second instinct, which was newer and therefore louder, was to say yes, and mean it.

"Yes," he said. "We'd love coffee. Joshua, we are staying for coffee. This is a small choice. This is me, choosing, in the present tense."

Joshua sat down, because Joshua always sits down when Kerry makes a good choice, as a way of celebrating it without making a speech.

The woman poured coffee into three cups that did not match, which Kerry loved, because matching cups are for people who have not been moved along, and mismatched cups are for people who have learned that a cup is a cup, as long as it holds coffee.

They talked. Not about the loop. Not about escape. Not about clocks or doors or rules. Chapter 131 — Five-ThirteenPublished October 29, 2026 · Read

Kerry did not notice the time change at first, because noticing time had become a dangerous habit. In the dead end, time was a rumor, a joke, a clock stuck at 5:12 that refused to apologize for being stuck. You learned not to look at it too closely, the way you learn not to look directly at a streetlight that is flickering in a rhythm that is almost, but not quite, a song.

But Joshua noticed. Joshua always notices the important thing half a second before Kerry does, which is both annoying and the entire reason Kerry is still alive, still laughing, still holding somebody's hand at an hour that is technically morning but feels like a rumor.

"Kerry," Joshua said, very quietly, in the voice he uses when he does not want to scare a good thing away. "Look."

Kerry looked at Joshua's phone. He expected 5:12. He had earned the right to expect 5:12. He had lived at 5:12, slept at 5:12, eaten breakfast at 5:12 on a Tuesday that was also last Tuesday and also every Tuesday, and he had made his peace with 5:12 the way you make peace with a roommate who never pays rent and never leaves: you stop asking him to leave, and you start charging him in stories instead.

The phone did not say 5:12.

It said 5:13.

Kerry stared at it. He stared at it the way he had stared at the DEAD END sign on the first night, the way he had stared at a tent that was his tent and also not his tent, the way he had stared at a wall that was laughing and practicing how to laugh properly. He stared at it like it might change its mind if he looked away, and like it might be a trick, and like it might be the most beautiful thing he had ever seen, all at once, because it was all three.

"5:13," Kerry said, out loud, just to hear how it sounded in real Hollywood air. "Joshua. It's 5:13."

"I know," Joshua said. "I checked twice. I checked three times, actually, because the first time I thought my eyes were lying, and the second time I thought the phone was lying, and the third time I decided that if both my eyes and my phone were lying in exactly the same way, I was going to believe the lie, because it was a very good lie."

It was not a lie. It was one minute past stuck. One minute past the loop. One minute past the place where the street had kept them, politely, patiently, at the same time, for what felt like a week and a year at the same time.

One minute does not sound like much. One minute is a commercial break. One minute is the time it takes to fold a tent badly, or to tell a short joke, or to wait for coffee that is ten minutes away, which in outreach time means anywhere from ten minutes to the heat death of the universe. One minute, in real life, is nothing.

But one minute past stuck is everything. One minute past stuck is, technically, unstuck. And unstuck, Kerry was learning, is a kind of freedom — not the loud kind of freedom, not the kind with fireworks and a parade and a man arguing with a parking meter about a ticket he definitely deserved, but the quiet kind, the kind that fits in your pocket next to a notebook and a note in your own handwriting and a transfer ticket that is also a map and also a joke, depending on how you hold it up to the light.

They stood there, on a real street, in real Hollywood, at 5:13, holding hands, holding their breath, holding the minute like it was a small, warm animal that might run away if they squeezed too hard.

"Do you feel different?" Joshua asked.

Kerry thought about it. He thought about it the way he thinks about everything important: out loud, in a circle, until the circle lands somewhere useful. "I feel the same," he said. "And I feel completely different. Both. At the same time. Which, I believe, is the loop's favorite paradox, and also the real world's favorite paradox, because real life is just a loop with better coffee and worse timing."

Joshua laughed, and his laugh did not echo down a dead end and come back sounding just a little bit different, like it had picked up a friend on the way. It echoed down a real street and came back sounding like itself, which was, after everything, a relief and a small disappointment, because Kerry had gotten used to laughs that brought friends home with them.

"Okay," Kerry said. "New rule. We celebrate 5:13. We do not make a big deal about it, because big deals scare good minutes away, but we notice it, and we remember it, and we tell it, later, to people who need to hear that stuck is not forever, even when stuck feels forever, even when stuck has a clock and a sign and a polite cop telling you to move along."

Joshua squeezed his hand. "And what do we do at 5:14?"

Kerry grinned, because grinning was the only honest response available, and because grinning at 5:13 felt like a prayer and a joke at the same time. "At 5:14," he said, "we keep walking. We walk like people who have somewhere to go, even if that somewhere is just the next curb, and the next coffee, and the next joke. We walk, and we do not run, because running is still against the rules, even out here, especially out here, because running is what you do when you are afraid of staying, and we are not afraid of staying anymore."

They walked. The sky over Hollywood was still deciding what color to be, which was normal, which was real, which was almost dawn and almost night and almost something else, and Kerry, who had spent a loop learning to read a sky that was deciding, decided, for once, not to read it at all. He just walked under it, hand in hand, at 5:13, one minute past stuck, one minute into freedom, one minute into the rest of the story, which was, he suspected, going to be funnier, and scarier, and truer than anything that had come before.

Probably all three. Probably at the same time.

Probably, he thought, as the minute ticked over, quietly, politely, without asking permission, that was exactly the point.

Chapter 132 — The Minute, Past StuckPublished October 29, 2026 · Read

Past stuck, the city moved differently. Kerry noticed it first in the traffic, which is a strange place to notice a miracle, but Hollywood is a strange place to live, and miracles, Kerry had learned, do not always arrive with trumpets. Sometimes they arrive with traffic, moving at a normal speed, in a normal direction, past a normal curb, where two normal men are sitting, holding hands, trying not to make a big deal out of a minute.

Before the loop, traffic had been an enemy. Traffic was noise, and exhaust, and proof that everybody else had somewhere to go and Kerry did not, or that everybody else had a car and Kerry had a tent, or that everybody else was moving and Kerry was being moved along. Traffic, before, was the sound of the city telling him to hurry up, even when he had nowhere to hurry to.

Past stuck, traffic sounded different. It sounded like a city that was moving with him, not against him. It sounded like a song he had finally learned the words to, even if he was still singing them slightly off-key, which is, Kerry maintained, the correct way to sing any song worth singing.

"We're moving with it," Joshua said, watching a bus go by. It was not the loop bus. It did not come around the block and return him to the same stop. It went past, and kept going, which was, after the loop, the most exciting thing a bus had ever done. "Do you feel that? We're not fighting the city anymore. We're just... in it. Like we're part of the traffic, but on foot, and funnier."

Kerry nodded. He felt it in his legs, which were not running, which were walking, steadily, at a pace that was neither hurried nor stuck. He felt it in his shoulders, which had been up around his ears since the first move-along, and which were now, slowly, coming down, like a tent being folded carefully, instead of in a panic, in the dark, in under two minutes, while a policeman watched.

He felt it, most of all, in his laugh. His laugh, past stuck, did not have to be brave. It did not have to cover fear. It could just be a laugh, a real laugh, the kind you laugh when you see a man arguing with a parking meter and you realize, with a sudden, warm clarity, that you have been that man, and that the parking meter has won, every time, and that losing to a parking meter is, in its own way, a very human thing to do.

They walked past the spot where the loop had been, or where the dead end had been, or where a street that did not exist had once existed, and Kerry did not look for it. He did not need to look for it. Looking for it was what you did when you were still in it. Walking past it, calmly, without checking, was what you did when you were past it, even if past it did not mean gone forever, even if past it just meant one minute past, and one minute was enough, for now, for today, for this walk.

"Do you think we'll go back?" Joshua asked, and his voice was careful, the way his voice gets when he is asking a question he already knows the answer to, but wants to hear Kerry say it out loud, because saying it out loud makes it real.

"Probably," Kerry said, honestly, because honesty was the only currency that had never run out in the loop, and he was not about to stop spending it now. "Everybody returns, eventually. The sign said COME BACK SOON, and the sign, for all its faults, was not lying. But returning is different from being stuck. Returning is a choice. Stuck is what happens when you don't get to choose. And today, Joshua, today we choose. Today we walk, and tomorrow we might visit, and next month we might check up on the street, like a checkup, like a friend, but today, we are past stuck, and past stuck is a place, not just a time, and I intend to live in it for a while."

Joshua smiled, and his smile was the kind of smile that makes a real street feel like a home, even when home is still a word you are learning how to use without flinching.

"Past stuck," Joshua repeated, trying it on, like a new jacket, like a new joke, like a new name. "I like it. It sounds like a neighborhood. It sounds like somewhere you could get mail, if you had an address, which we don't, yet, but we will, because past stuck is the kind of place where addresses happen, slowly, and then all at once."

They kept walking, with the city, not against it, past traffic that moved, past sirens that were real, past a man arguing with a parking meter who was, Kerry was delighted to note, arguing about a completely different ticket than last Tuesday's ticket, which meant time was moving, and tickets were moving, and Kerry was moving, and all of it, together, was a kind of music.

A minute past stuck, Kerry thought, is not a destination. It is a direction. And directions, unlike destinations, do not run out. You just keep walking in them, hand in hand, laughing, not running, not counting, not answering anything you do not want to answer, until the direction becomes a life.

And that, for now, was enough. That, for now, was everything.

Chapter 133 — The Nod, Off DutyPublished October 29, 2026 · Read

The cop was not on duty. Kerry could tell, because the cop was not holding a flashlight, and he was not holding a clipboard, and he was not saying the speech, and he was not standing in the particular way cops stand when they are about to tell you to move along, which is a stance Kerry knew by heart, the way you know a song you have heard too many times, even when you wish you did not know it at all.

The cop was sitting on a curb. He was eating a sandwich. He was eating it the way tired men eat sandwiches, which is to say, quickly, and gratefully, and without making eye contact with anybody, because eye contact, at lunch, is an invitation to conversation, and conversation, at lunch, is an invitation to work, and work, at lunch, is the last thing a tired man wants.

Kerry saw him, and Kerry stopped, and Joshua stopped, because Joshua always stops when Kerry stops, even when Kerry stops for a reason Joshua does not yet understand, which is the definition of love, or at least a very good working definition.

"Is that —" Joshua started.

"Yes," Kerry said. "That's him. Or that's almost him. Or that's him, off duty, which is a different person, in the same way that I am a different person when I am not being moved along, which is to say, the same person, but softer around the edges."

The cop looked up. He saw Kerry. He saw Joshua. He saw two men holding hands on a real street at a time that was no longer 5:12, and for a second, Kerry was sure the cop was going to stand up, and reach for a flashlight he was not carrying, and say the speech, because speeches are habits, and habits are hard to break, even off duty, especially off duty.

Instead, the cop nodded.

It was a small nod. It was not a wave. It was not a smile, exactly, although there was something around the eyes that might have been a smile, or might have been sandwich-related happiness, which is a real and valid kind of happiness. It was a nod that said: I see you. I am not on duty. You are not in trouble. We are both just men, sitting and standing, on a curb and on a street, in a city that is still deciding what color the sky should be.

Kerry nodded back. He nodded back the way you nod back to a gift, carefully, gratefully, without making a big deal about it, because big deals scare good nods away.

They walked on, and Kerry kept the nod. He kept it the way he kept jokes, and stories, and Joshua's hand, which was still in his, which was, if he was being honest, the real miracle here — not the nod, not the minute past stuck, not the city moving with him, but the fact that through a loop, and a dead end, and a clock stuck at 5:12, and a wall that laughed, and a third knock, and a landlord who charged rent in stories, Joshua's hand had stayed in his, and had never, not once, let go first.

"Did you see that?" Joshua asked, after they had walked a little way, after the curb and the sandwich and the nod were behind them, but not gone, because good things, Kerry was learning, do not go away just because you walk past them. They stay, in your pocket, next to the notebook and the note and the transfer ticket.

"I saw it," Kerry said. "A nod from an off-duty cop is a gift. I am keeping it. I am putting it in the notebook, under 'Gifts, Unexpected,' right next to the coffee that stayed hot, and the tent that was there yesterday, and the laugh that practiced until it got it right."

Joshua laughed. "You have a section in your notebook called 'Gifts, Unexpected'?"

"I do now," Kerry said. "I just invented it, for the nod. The nod is the first entry. The second entry will be whatever good thing happens next, and the third entry will be whatever good thing happens after that, and by the end of the year, the notebook will be full of unexpected gifts, which will be a problem, because then I will need a second notebook, and a second notebook is a commitment, and I am not afraid of commitments anymore, I am just saying, notebooks add up."

They walked on, nodding at strangers, not because strangers deserved nods, although they did, but because nodding, Kerry had learned, is a way of saying: I see you, I am not on duty, you are not in trouble, we are both just people, on a street, in a city, at a time that is moving again.

And the city, for its part, nodded back, in traffic, and in sirens, and in a man arguing with a parking meter who, for once, looked up, and nodded, too, like a man off duty from his own argument, at last.

That nod, Kerry thought, was almost as good as the cop's nod. Almost. But not quite. Because the cop's nod was the first nod that did not come with a speech attached, and a nod without a speech is a kind of freedom, too, quiet, and small, and worth keeping.

He kept it. He kept it all the way home, wherever home turned out to be, which, for now, was wherever Joshua's hand was, and wherever a nod could be given, and received, without anybody having to move along.

Chapter 134 — The Real Hollywood, AgainPublished October 29, 2026 · Read

Real Hollywood, again, was louder than Kerry remembered, and also quieter, which is a contradiction, and also the truth, because real Hollywood, after the loop, is both: louder in traffic, and quieter in the places that matter, like the space between two people holding hands, and the pause before a joke lands, and the moment after a nod, when nobody says anything, because nothing needs to be said.

The traffic was real. Kerry checked, because checking was a habit, and habits, even strange ones, can be good, if they remind you that you survived something. The traffic moved, and honked, and stopped, and moved again, and none of it repeated itself exactly, which was new, and which was a relief, because repetition, polite or not, gets old, even when it is funny, especially when it is funny.

The sirens were real. They were far away, and they were close, and they were somebody else's emergency, which is a terrible thing to be grateful for, and Kerry was grateful anyway, because somebody else's emergency meant it was not his emergency, not today, not at 5:13, not on a morning when he was, for once, just walking, not running, not being moved along, not answering knocks.

And the man arguing with the parking meter was real. He was arguing about a new ticket, with new words, in a new order, and Kerry laughed, because real life, after the loop, is the funniest thing of all. Real life does not need a loop to be funny. Real life is funny on its own, in the way a man argues with a machine that cannot argue back, and loses, and argues anyway, because arguing is how you know you are still here, still awake, still alive enough to be annoyed by a ticket.

"Welcome back," Joshua said, gesturing at the street, at the traffic, at the sirens, at the man and his meter, like a tour guide showing off a city he loves, even when the city has not always loved him back. "Real Hollywood. Population: us, plus everybody else, plus one very opinionated pigeon, who is, I note, still here, still crossing the street, still not laughing, which makes it the loop's only honest critic, and also real Hollywood's only honest critic, because critics, real critics, never laugh at the thing they are criticizing, they just watch, and judge, and cross the street, slowly, with great dignity."

Kerry laughed, and his laugh, in real Hollywood, sounded different than it had sounded in the loop. In the loop, his laugh had echoed, and come back changed, like it had picked up a friend. In real Hollywood, his laugh went out, and came back as itself, which was, after everything, a kind of homecoming. A laugh that comes back as itself is a laugh you can trust. A laugh that comes back changed is a laugh you have to get to know all over again, which is fun, but also work, and Kerry had done enough work, for now.

They found coffee. Real coffee, from a place that was open, that served coffee, that took cash, which Kerry paid with cash, not with a story, because real Hollywood, thank God, still takes cash, and stories, in real Hollywood, are for telling, not for paying, although Kerry suspected, and would later confirm, that stories, told well, can buy you almost anything, including coffee, including a second cup, including a seat by the window, which is funny, because there was a window, this time, a real one, with real light coming through it, and real people on the other side of it, living real lives.

"This is real," Kerry said, holding the cup with both hands, like a man holding a small, warm animal. "This is real coffee, in a real cup, on a real street, at a real time, which is now, I think, 5:47, or 6:02, or some other time that is not 5:12, and I am not going to check, because checking is how you get stuck, and I am past stuck, and past stuck people do not check the time every five seconds, they just drink the coffee, and enjoy it, and trust that time will do what time does, which is move, slowly, and then all at once."

Joshua, who had checked, because Joshua always checks, said, "It's 6:04," and then, seeing Kerry's face, added, "But I won't tell you again, unless you ask, and you won't ask, because you are past stuck, and past stuck people are very dignified about time, except when they are not, which is most of the time, which is fine."

They drank. They walked. They watched real Hollywood be real, which is to say, messy, and loud, and funny, and a little bit sad, and a lot a bit hopeful, all at once, the way real places are, when you have spent long enough in an unreal place to appreciate the mess.

And Kerry, who had once thought real Hollywood was the place that moved him along, realized, with a warmth that surprised him, that real Hollywood was also the place that had taught him to laugh, and to hold hands, and to tell stories, and to stay, even when staying was hard, especially when staying was hard.

Real Hollywood, again, was not a return. It was a reunion. And reunions, Kerry thought, as he finished his coffee, and held Joshua's hand, and walked into a morning that was finally, blessedly, moving, are the best kind of homecoming, because they remind you that you left, and that you came back, and that coming back, on purpose, is a choice, and choices, made well, are a kind of freedom.

Chapter 135 — The Laugh, Real LifePublished October 29, 2026 · Read

Laughing at real life, Kerry realized, was different than laughing in the loop, and the difference mattered, and the difference was also the joke, because differences, in Kerry's experience, are always the joke, if you look at them the right way, which is sideways, and with love.

In the loop, laughter had been a tool. It had been a light, when the lights went out. It had been a currency, when cash would not work. It had been a key, when doors would not open. It had been a shield, when fear came knocking, three times, patiently, politely, waiting for an answer. Laughter, in the loop, had been useful, which is a strange thing to say about laughter, because laughter is supposed to be useless, and joyful, and free, and Kerry had made it useful, because he had needed it to be useful, to survive.

In real life, laughter did not need to be useful. It could just be laughter. It could be the laugh you laugh when you see a pigeon cross the street with great dignity, and you realize the pigeon is judging you, and you deserve to be judged, because you are a man holding a coffee cup with both hands, on a real street, at a real time, laughing at a pigeon, which is, objectively, a ridiculous thing to do, and also, subjectively, the best thing Kerry had done all day.

"You're laughing at real life," Joshua said, watching him, with the fond exasperation of a man who has watched Kerry laugh at real life many times, and has never once been disappointed by it. "Not at the loop. Not at a wall. Not at a street that laughs back. At real life. At a pigeon. At traffic. At a man arguing with a parking meter about a ticket he definitely deserved, and will definitely argue about again tomorrow, because that is what men do, when they have a parking meter, and a ticket, and a morning to fill."

"I am," Kerry said, laughing harder, because laughing about laughing is the loop's favorite trick, and also real life's favorite trick, and Kerry, who had learned both tricks, was now fluent in both. "And do you know what I realized, laughing at real life? The loop did not make me funny. I thought it did. I thought the dead end had given me a sense of humor, like a gift, like a charger that fits no phone, like a notebook with a sentence in my own handwriting on page three. But it didn't. It revealed that I already was funny. I was funny before the loop, I was funny in the loop, and I am funny after the loop, because funny is not a place, Joshua. Funny is a person. And that person, inconveniently, and wonderfully, is me."

Joshua nodded, like a man hearing a revelation he has known all along, and has been waiting, patiently, for Kerry to catch up to. "I knew that," he said. "I have always known that. You were funny when we had nothing, and you were funny when we had a tent, and you were funny when we had a dead end, and you are funny now, when we have coffee, and a street, and a minute past stuck. Funny is not something the loop gave you. Funny is something you brought into the loop, and the loop, being a polite host, gave it back to you, a little warmer, a little louder, a little more practiced, like the laugh in the wall, which practiced until it got it right."

That revelation, like all good revelations, was both a relief and a responsibility. A relief, because it meant Kerry did not have to go back to the loop to be funny. He could be funny here, on a real street, with real coffee, with real people, who laughed, and who went quiet, in the good way, when a true story landed. A responsibility, because it meant funny was his, now, not borrowed, not rented, not paid for in stories, but owned, outright, like a joke you tell so many times it becomes yours, even if you heard it somewhere else first.

"So what do I do with it?" Kerry asked, honestly, because honesty, after the loop, was still the only currency that never ran out. "If I'm responsible for my own funniness now, what do I do? Do I tell it on corners? Do I tell it on stages? Do I write it down, so others can find it, the way I found notes in my own handwriting, left by a version of myself I had not met yet?"

Joshua took his hand, which was, Kerry thought, the correct answer to almost every question worth asking. "You do all of it," Joshua said. "You tell it on corners, and on stages, and on pages, and you tell it to me, first, always, because I am your first audience, and your best audience, and your audience who laughs even when the joke is bad, which is not often, but it happens, and I laugh anyway, because I love you, and because bad jokes, told with love, are still jokes, and still count."

Kerry laughed, at real life, at Joshua, at himself, at the pigeon, who was still crossing the street, still judging, still not laughing, which made Kerry laugh harder, because a critic who never laughs is the funniest critic of all.

Chapter 171 — The Growing Up, FeltPublished October 29, 2026 · Read

Growing up, Kerry had always thought, would feel like a graduation. A ceremony. Somebody handing you a piece of paper and saying, congratulations, you are now an adult, please do not lose this paper, because you will need it for jobs and apartments and other adult mysteries.

It did not feel like that at all.

It felt like this: standing in a street that had taught him how to laugh when he was scared, holding Joshua's hand, and realizing that leaving easily was still leaving, and easy goodbyes were still goodbyes, and goodbyes, even the good kind, still stung a little in the chest, like a joke that lands a second too late.

"I thought this would feel bigger," Kerry said.

Joshua squeezed his hand. "It is big. You're just used to it now. That's what growing up is. The big thing stops feeling big because you've been carrying it long enough that your arms got strong."

"That's either very wise or a very fancy way of saying I've gotten used to weird streets," Kerry said.

"Both," Joshua said. "Growing up is both. Always both."

They walked the dead end one more time, slowly, not because they had to, but because walking slowly is how you say thank you to a place without having to make a speech about it. Kerry looked at the sign. DEAD END. It had not changed. He had. That seemed fair, and also a little unfair, because signs get to stay the same forever, and people have to do all the changing, and nobody pays people for that work.

The cat crossed their path, one eye bright, the other one closed like it was keeping a secret, which it was, probably, because cats always are. Kerry crouched down.

"Hey," he said. "I know you don't do goodbyes. I know you do that thing where you just walk away mid-conversation like you remembered an appointment. So I'm not going to make a big deal out of this. I'm just going to say it plainly, the way you would want it, if cats wanted things said plainly, which they don't, but I'm doing it anyway."

The cat stared at him.

"Thank you," Kerry said. "For leading us. For not leading us, when not leading us was the lesson. For being the only thing in here that never repeated itself, which, now that I think about it, is the best compliment I have ever given a cat, and I have given a lot of compliments to cats."

The cat blinked its one eye, slowly, which in cat language is either I love you or I am tolerating you, and in this cat's language, Kerry decided, it was both.

Next was the vendor, with his cart and his bell and his pockets full of things nobody remembered buying. Kerry had expected him to be older, or younger, or both, and he was, in the way the dead end did ages, which is to say, unhelpfully and completely.

"You again," the vendor said, ringing his bell once, politely. "Or you, for the first time, depending on which loop we're counting, which we are not, because counting loops is forbidden, and also pointless."

"I wanted to say goodbye properly," Kerry said. "And thank you. For the notebook. For the charger that fit no phone. For remembering me before I remembered you, which was creepy, and then later, was kind."

The vendor nodded, like a man accepting a payment he had already spent. "You paid already," he said. "In stories. "Leaving easily," the landlord said, when he saw them, "is still leaving. Don't pretend it isn't, or you'll come back here in a month wondering why your chest hurts, and I'll have to charge you a story to explain it."

At the mention of the laugh, the street did something it had not done in a while. It laughed back. Not the big warm laugh from the first night. A smaller laugh. A quieter one. "See?" Joshua said, softly. "Even the street feels it. Growing up isn't a graduation. It's a goodbye you say properly, and then you walk out, and you don't look back, except you do look back, once, because you're human."

Kerry looked back, once.

The street looked back, in the way only a street can, which is to say, it did nothing at all, and somehow that was the kindest part.

"Okay," Kerry said, turning forward again, holding Joshua's hand tighter. "I'm grown up now. Or grown up enough. Or growing up, felt, right here, in my chest, where goodbyes live."

"Grown up enough is grown up," Joshua said. "Nobody gets the full version. The full version is a scam. The felt version is the real one."

They walked toward the mouth of the dead end, toward real Hollywood, toward traffic and sirens and a man arguing with a parking meter about a ticket he definitely deserved, and Kerry felt it all the way: the bittersweet, the easy, the hard, the goodbye, the growing up, felt, like a hand on his shoulder, like a laugh in the next room, like a story he would tell for the rest of his life, starting now.

Rent day in the dead end had always been a performance. The landlord would appear, or be there already, which was the same thing, and he would smile his charming, reasonable, impossible smile, and Kerry would tell a story, and Joshua would tell a joke, and the street would listen, and the rent would be paid, in laughter and in truth, and everybody would go on with their loop.

This rent day was different, because it was the last one.

Landlords in real life definitely don't waive. What's the catch? Is the catch a second landlord? Is there a second landlord hiding behind you?"

"There is no catch," the landlord said. "You have paid in full. In laughter, and in truth. Do you know how many tenants pay in full? Almost none. Most pay in jokes, which are lovely, but jokes are small change. You paid in truth, which is the only currency that doesn't lose value. And in laughter, which is the only currency that gains value when you spend it."

Kerry stared at him. "So we're paid up? We're done? We're not in arrears to a magic street?"

"You are paid in full," the landlord said, and then he did something Kerry had never seen him do. He looked almost human. Not human, exactly — landlords in the dead end are never exactly human, that would be too easy — but almost. His shoulders dropped a little. His smile dropped a little, too, into something sadder, and kinder, and more real.

"And almost sad," Kerry said, before he could stop himself, because his mouth sometimes says true things before his brain has approved them.

"Almost sad," the landlord agreed, and he did not argue, which made him, Kerry thought, the most dangerous person he had met in the dead end, and also, today, the saddest, and those two things, together, were a lot to carry for one landlord.

"Well," Kerry said, because somebody had to fill the silence, and it was usually him. "If we're paid in full, then I guess this is it. Last rent. No receipt, I assume? Because receipts in the dead end are notes in my own handwriting, and I already have too many of those."

Gently closing doors are better than slamming ones. So today, he closed gently.

The loop's door was not a normal door. It was not wood, or metal, or even, strictly speaking, a door. It was the feeling at the mouth of the dead end, where the real street met the unreal street, where Hollywood hummed and the dead end listened, where 5:12 met every other time, and tried, politely, to get along.

"Okay," Kerry said. "Gentle. Not slammed. Not rushed. Gentle."

The loop, grateful, did not lock it behind him.

Unlocked doors are invitations. Kerry had learned that in the dead end, where a locked door meant a lesson you had not earned yet, and an unlocked door meant a lesson you were ready for, or a room you were welcome in, or a joke you were finally allowed to hear the punchline to.

The loop's door, closed gently, unlocked, was the biggest invitation he had ever received, and he carried it the way you carry an invitation to a party you are not sure you will attend: in your pocket, carefully, where it cannot get wet, or lost, or accidentally thrown away with the receipts.

He kept it next to the transfer ticket, which was still a map, and a key, and a joke, depending on how you held it up to the light, and next to the map of streets that did not exist, which the vendor had given him, and next to the joke he had saved for a rainy day, which was a good joke to save, because rainy days need jokes more than sunny days do, and everybody knows it, except rainy days, which are too busy raining to know anything.

"Show me your pocket," Joshua said, one evening, in real Hollywood, on a real curb, eating real food that was not perfect, which made it perfect in a different way.

Kerry emptied his pocket onto the curb, carefully, like a man showing a museum collection: transfer ticket, map, joke, and, invisible but present, the invitation of the unlocked door.

"That's a lot of pocket," Joshua said.

"It's a lot of story," Kerry said. "And the invitation is the best part, because an invitation you don't have to use is the freest kind of invitation. If I had to go back, it would be a summons. If I could never go back, it would be a loss. But I can go back, when I want to, and I don't want to right now, and that wanting-not-to, freely chosen, is a kind of home."

Joshua picked up the transfer ticket and held it up to the streetlight. "Still a map," he said. Then he turned it sideways. "Still a key." Then he turned it upside down. "Still a joke. A very good joke, actually. The kind of joke that only gets funnier when you hold it upside down."

Kerry laughed, and the laugh echoed a little, down the real street, and came back sounding just a little bit different, like it had picked up a friend on the way, which was a dead-end laugh habit, and Kerry was glad some habits survived the move out, because good habits are worth keeping, even when they come from strange streets.

"Do you ever worry," Joshua asked, quieter now, "that you'll lose the invitation? That one day you'll reach into your pocket and it'll be gone, and the door will be locked, and you'll be just a man on a curb in Hollywood, with no magic street to go back to?"

Kerry thought about it, honestly, because Joshua deserved honest answers, especially about pockets and invitations and magic streets.

"Yes," Kerry said. "I worry about that. I worry about it the way I worry about losing my phone charger, which is to say, constantly, and also not really, because I know I will find another charger, or another story, or another door. The invitation isn't really in my pocket. The invitation is in my head, and in my stories, and in the way I tell them. You can't lose a story by keeping it in your pocket. You can only lose it by never telling it."

"So tell it," Joshua said.

So Kerry told it, right there, on the curb, to Joshua, who had already heard it, and who listened anyway, because listening to a story you have already heard, told by somebody you love, is not boring. It is a ritual. It is a door, unlocked, opened again, just to prove it still opens.

When he finished, Kerry put everything back in his pocket, carefully, in the same order: ticket, map, joke, invitation. "Okay," Kerry said, standing up, brushing off his knees, which is a very tenant thing to do, and also a very landlord thing to do, and Kerry was both, now, in a way. "Invitation kept. Door unlocked. Pocket full. Let's go home, wherever home is tonight, which is wherever we are holding hands, which is here, which is good."

Joshua took his hand. "Home is here," he agreed. "And also, in your pocket, next to the joke. That's a lot of homes for one man. You're a rich man, Kerry. Rich in homes, and jokes, and unlocked doors."

Wanting to visit is different from needing to. Kerry had learned that difference the way he learned most differences: by needing something desperately, for a long time, and then, one day, not needing it desperately anymore, and being surprised to find that he still wanted it, quietly, on purpose, like a song you choose to play, not a song that gets stuck in your head.

He wanted to visit the dead end, sometimes. Not every day. Not urgently. Sometimes, on quiet nights, when the city was loud.

That was the paradox of real Hollywood: it was loud, and it was lonely, at the same time. You leave when you're ready. That's a visit."

"Exactly," Kerry said. "And I want to visit, sometimes, on quiet nights, when I miss the street that listened. I don't want to move back in. I don't want to pay rent again, even in stories, even though I like stories. They talked about it for a while, the way couples talk about visits: when, how long, what to bring, whether to bring the cat, which was a joke, because you do not bring a cat anywhere, the cat brings itself, if it feels like it, which it usually does not, except when it does, which is always a surprise.

"We could go tomorrow," Joshua said. "Or next week. Or never, and just want to, which is also a kind of visit, if you think about it. Wanting to visit, held in your heart, is like visiting in your head, which is cheaper, and warmer, and you don't have to find parking."

Kerry laughed. "Wanting as visiting. That's a very dead-end idea. The street would love that. The street would say, 'Yes, wanting counts, wanting is a visit, wanting is a story, stories are rent, rent is paid,' and then it would charge me a story for wanting, which is fair, because wanting is a story too."

And later, when Kerry fell asleep, he dreamed of the dead end, not the scary version, not the looping version, but the listening version, the quiet version, the version where the streetlight was steady and warm, like a porch light left on for somebody coming home late, and in the dream, he visited, and the street welcomed him, and he said, "I wanted to come, not needed to," and the street laughed, warmly, and said, in its own way, without words, "Wanting is the best reason. "Did you visit?" Joshua asked, sleepily.

"In a dream," Kerry said. "Which counts. Dream visits are visits. The street knows that. I know that. You know that, because you're smiling too."

Joshua was smiling too. "Wanting to visit," he said, "is a good habit. Keep it. Habits, even strange ones, can be good, if they remind you that you have a place to go back to, and a choice about whether to go."

Kerry kept it.
