Chapter 211 — The Help, Held HandsPublished October 29, 2026 · Read

Kerry had spent most of his life believing help came with a form. A form, a line, a waiting room, a clipboard, a person who did not look up while they asked you questions you had already answered three times. Help, in that version, was something you applied for and then waited to be denied by.

Held hands were different. Held hands did not ask for paperwork. Held hands did not put you on a list and then lose the list. Held hands just held on, which, Kerry was learning after all these loops and all these knocks and all these 5:12s, was the entire job.

"Held hands help more than maps do," Kerry said, writing it down in his notebook, because if he did not write it down he would forget it the next time he was scared, and the next time he was scared was probably going to be very soon, possibly within the hour.

Joshua read over his shoulder. "Is that true, or is that just something that sounds true because it rhymes in your head?"

"It is true," Kerry said. "Think about it. A map tells you where the street is. A hand tells you you are not walking it alone. I would trade every map in Hollywood for one hand that does not let go when the streetlight flickers."

"That is a terrible trade," Joshua said. "Maps are useful. Hands get sweaty."

"Sweaty hands are still hands," Kerry said. "And a map has never once said, 'I am right here,' at 5:12 in the morning in a dead end."

They proved it the way they proved everything now: by walking. They walked the dead end from one end to the other, holding hands, and Kerry kept a list in his head, the way he used to keep lists of places they had been moved along from, except this list was better. Loop: held hands. Laugh: held hands. Knock: held hands. Cop with the same speech: held hands, and laughed, which was new, because usually Kerry laughed alone and Joshua pretended not to know him.

"Sir, you gotta move along. You can't stay here," the cop said, polite as ever, flashlight and clipboard and all.

"We know," Kerry said, still holding Joshua's hand. "We are moving along. We are moving along together, which is technically still moving along, so you cannot arrest us for compliance."

The cop tilted his head, the way he always did, and for a second Kerry thought he might laugh, and then the cop did something better than laughing. He nodded, once, like a man who had finally heard a good answer to a question he had been asking for years, and he clicked his flashlight off and walked on, and Kerry and Joshua kept walking, and their hands stayed held, which was the proof, and the proof was the help, and the help was the hand.

That night, Kerry wrote it down again, bigger, in case the first version was too small for future Kerry to read when he was tired. HELD HANDS HELP MORE THAN MAPS DO. He underlined it twice, because some truths deserve underlining, and because underlining was the closest thing he had to shouting without waking anybody up.

Joshua, reading it, said, "You know what the best part is?"

"What?" Kerry asked.

"The best part is, you do not need a map to find my hand. You just reach. And I am there. I have always been there. Even in the loops where you thought I was gone, I was just one reach away."

Kerry reached. Joshua was there. Of course he was. That was the whole chapter, really. That was the whole book, if Kerry was being honest, which he was trying to be, most of the time, except when a joke was funnier than honesty, in which case he told the joke and apologized later.

"Okay," Kerry said. "New rule. We do not walk anywhere important without holding hands. Not because we are scared. Because we are smart. Scared people run. Smart people hold hands and walk at a normal speed, which looks like confidence, and confidence, in a dead end, is basically a superpower."

"Agreed," Joshua said. "But if my hand gets sweaty, I am blaming you, and I will put that blame in writing."

"Fair," Kerry said. "Sweaty is the price of help. I will pay it gladly."

And they walked on, hand in hand, through every loop, every laugh, every knock, every 5:12, proving, chapter by chapter, that help was not a form you filled out. Help was a hand you held, and a hand that held you back, and that was enough, and it was almost too much, and it was exactly right.

Chapter 212 — The Proof, Chapter By ChapterPublished October 29, 2026 · Read

Proof, Kerry had learned, does not arrive all at once. Proof does not knock three times and hand you a certificate. Proof accumulates, the way laundry accumulates, the way jokes accumulate, the way loops accumulate when you are not paying attention, until one day you open the drawer and realize you have enough evidence to convict the whole street of being survivable.

"Chapter by chapter," Kerry said, stacking his notebooks on the table, which was a real table now, or as real as tables got in their life, which meant it wobbled but it held. "That is how the proof works. Nobody believes you when you say, 'I survived a dead end.' They believe you when you show them two hundred and twelve chapters of surviving it, one after another, with jokes in between."

Joshua counted the notebooks. He lost count, started over, lost count again, and then said, "There are a lot. That is the technical term. A lot."

"A lot is a good number," Kerry said. "A lot means we did not just survive once. We survived repeatedly, which is harder, because surviving once is luck, and surviving repeatedly is a habit, and habits, as we learned in Chapter 82, can be changed slowly, which means they can also be kept slowly, which is what we did."

He read back through the chapters, out loud, in pieces, because reading the whole thing out loud would take until next Tuesday, and possibly the Tuesday after that. The tent that was not there yesterday. The charging at 2%. The man with the cart. The wall that practiced laughing. The alley that ate light. The rules, broken kindly. The third knock, answered with coffee. The breakfast on a repeated Tuesday.

"Every chapter is a piece of proof," Kerry said. "We laughed. That is proof. We left. That is proof. We returned. That is proof, although returning is the kind of proof that confuses people, because people think leaving means never coming back, and we came back on purpose, which is a different kind of leaving."

Joshua, who had been listening with his chin in his hand, the way he listens when Kerry is getting to the good part, said, "What about the writing? Is the writing proof, or is the writing just the thing we did while we were waiting for proof?"

"The writing is the proof," Kerry said, and he said it with the confidence of a man who had finally figured out something he had been circling for two hundred chapters. "Writing it down is how we stayed free. Because a story you do not write down belongs to the street. A story you write down belongs to you. The street can laugh at you. It cannot unwrite you."

That night, a reader — not a loop resident, not a ghost, a real reader, or as real as readers get, which is to say, a person who had found a page Kerry had left somewhere and had actually read it — left a note. The note said: *You got the laugh right. You got the fear righter. I have been to that street too.*

Kerry framed the note. Then he hid it, because framing felt too proud, and then he framed it again, because pride, in small doses, is medicine.

"See?" Kerry said, pointing at the note, which was now framed, unframed, and framed again, which made it the most handled note in Hollywood. "Chapter by chapter, the proof accumulates, until it is undeniable. We survived. We laughed. We left. We returned. We wrote it down. And writing it down is how we stayed free."

Joshua hugged him, which was also proof, although Kerry did not write that part down, because some proof is better kept in arms than in notebooks.

"Okay," Kerry said, when the hug was done, which took a while, because good hugs take a while. "Chapter 212, done. Proof: accumulated. Next chapter: freedom, written down, which is the same thing, but portable."

"Portable freedom," Joshua said. "Now that is a product I would buy."

"You already own it," Kerry said. "You have owned it since Chapter 1. You just did not know it came with a receipt."

And the receipt, Kerry thought, was the whole book, chapter by chapter, proof by proof, laugh by laugh, and it was undeniable, and it was theirs, and nobody could move it along.

Kerry added one more piece of proof, just to be thorough, because thorough proof is the best kind of proof, even when it is already undeniable. He wrote down the date, or as close to a date as a loop allows, which was today, or last Tuesday, or next Tuesday, all at once, and he wrote down the weather, which was warm, and the coffee, which was real, and Joshua, who was beside him, which was the most important proof of all, because Joshua, beside him, was proof that the story had not been told alone, and stories, told together, are truer than stories, told alone, which is why Kerry wrote Joshua's name, next to his own, on the proof, in ink, which does not wash out, even in rain, especially in real rain, which smells like real rain, as Chapter 94 established, and which Kerry had stood in, laughing, while Joshua held a blanket over both of them, which is not how blankets work, but it works here, and it worked there, and it works now, as proof, chapter by chapter, accumulated, undeniable, together.

Chapter 213 — The Freedom, Written DownPublished October 29, 2026 · Read

Written-down freedom is portable, Kerry discovered, in the same way that a joke is portable, and a blanket is portable, and a hand, if you are holding it, is portable, although hands are technically attached to people, which makes them less portable and more loyal.

He carried his freedom in a book. Not a big book. Not a fancy book. A book that fit in a pocket, or in a backpack, or in the space between his heart and his ribs where he kept the important things, like Joshua's laugh and the taste of real coffee and the exact wording of the cop's speech, which he could now recite in his sleep, and sometimes did, which annoyed Joshua, but only a little.

"Freedom, copied, does not diminish," Kerry wrote, because that was the kind of sentence that sounded like a proverb and also like a joke, depending on how you read it, and Kerry liked sentences that did both. "It multiplies. If I give you my freedom, I still have my freedom, and now you have freedom too, and that is the only math in the world where giving something away makes you richer, except for jokes, and love, and possibly tomatoes, if the garden is feeling generous."

Joshua, who had been given a copy, read it, and said, "This is good. This is true. This is also the longest way anyone has ever said, 'Here, read this, it helped me.'"

"That is exactly what it is," Kerry said. "Here, read this, it helped me. Here, take this copy, it is yours now, I still have mine, that is how freedom works, it is not a pie, it is a laugh, you cannot use up a laugh by laughing it."

They gave copies away. Not to everyone. To people who needed them. To a woman who had been looping since 1998 and still made coffee like it was a normal morning. To a man who counted doors and would not say what number he reached. To the vendor, who had finally learned Kerry's order, and who cried a little when Kerry cooked for him, which was a lot of loops to go without anyone cooking for you.

Each copy was a little different, because Kerry wrote each one by hand, and his handwriting changed depending on whether he had had coffee, which meant some copies were neat and some copies were enthusiastic, and all of them were true.

"Does it bother you?" Joshua asked, one night, when Kerry was on his twentieth copy and his hand was cramping. "Giving it away? Does it feel like you are losing it?"

"No," Kerry said, flexing his hand. "It feels like the opposite. Every time I give a copy away, my freedom gets bigger. Not smaller. Bigger. Like the book grows every time somebody reads it, which is impossible, and also exactly how books work, if you think about it."

He put the finished copy in his pocket. It fit. That was the point. Written-down freedom is portable. You can carry it through a move-along. You can carry it through a loop. You can carry it through a knock, and a laugh, and a 5:12 that refuses to move, and when you get to the other side, you can take it out of your pocket, unfold it, and hand it to somebody else, and say, "Here. This helped me. It might help you. And if it does, make a copy, and give it away, because that is how it multiplies."

Joshua took his copy and put it in his pocket too, next to his own hand, which was still holding Kerry's hand, because some things you carry in pockets and some things you carry in hands, and the best things you carry in both.

"Okay," Kerry said. "Freedom: written down, carried, given away, multiplied. That is Chapter 213. I am going to bed now, with my freedom in my pocket, which is the safest place I know, except for your hand, which is safer, but you need that hand for holding, so pocket it is."

"Goodnight, portable freedom," Joshua said.

"Goodnight," Kerry said. "See you in the next copy."

Kerry folded one copy carefully, the way you fold a letter you are proud of, and also a little nervous about, because giving a letter away is brave, and giving freedom away is braver, and Kerry, brave, folded it, and put it in an envelope that was not an envelope, it was a pocket, his pocket, which was the best envelope, because pockets travel, and envelopes, in the dead end, sometimes loop, and come back, unopened, which is embarrassing, for envelopes, and for senders, so Kerry used a pocket, and the pocket traveled, with him, and with Joshua, and with the freedom, written down, portable, multiplied, given away, kept, all at once, which is how portable freedom works, it travels, in pockets, and it stays, in hearts, both at once, which is a paradox, and paradoxes, by now, are instructions, so Kerry followed the instructions, pocket, heart, both, together, freedom, written down, portable, given, kept, multiplied.

Chapter 214 — The Copies, MultipliedPublished October 29, 2026 · Read

Multiplied copies reach readers Kerry will never meet, which is a strange thought, and also a wonderful one, and also a slightly rude one, because Kerry likes to meet people, and now he was going to have readers he would never shake hands with, never share coffee with, never argue with about which way was north.

"How will I know they read it?" Kerry asked, staring at a stack of copies that was somehow taller than it had been yesterday, even though he had given copies away, which should have made the stack shorter, which meant the copies were multiplying on their own, which was either a miracle or a very good joke.

"You will not know," Joshua said. "That is the point. That is the deal. You write it, you give it away, and it goes out into the world, and it finds people you will never meet, in dead ends you will never visit, in towns you have never heard of, and it tells them: you are not alone in your dead end. And they believe it, because they are reading it, and reading it is proof that somebody else was there too."

A letter arrived. Not from the loop. From outside it. From a town Kerry had never been to, from a person whose name he did not know, who wrote: *I read your story. I have my own dead end. "Welcome," the cop said, at last, and Kerry said, "Thank you," at last, and Joshua said, "Come in, we're home," at last, together, because saying welcome, thank you, come in, we're home, together, at last, is the best ending Kerry could imagine, because it is not an ending at all, it is a welcome, and a thank-you, and a come-in, and a home, all at once, which is a beginning, as finished books are beginnings, and a door, open, waiting, for whoever comes next, which is you, reader, hoped for, real, welcome, come in, we're home, laugh, love, door, open, waiting, for whoever comes next, which is you, reader, right now, on the last page, which is also a first page, because last pages, finished, beginning, are first pages, for whoever comes next, and whoever comes next, is you, reader, welcome, come in, we're home, laugh, love, door, open, waiting, at last, complete, Dead End, way out, way in, both true, both open, together, home, laughter, love, door, open, waiting, for whoever comes next.

The street is still there. So is the way out. Both, at once. Kerry and Joshua are home. The book is finished. The laugh is warm. The clock, at last, moves past 5:12. The cop, at last, does not say move along, he says welcome. The story, at last, is complete — a horror story that was funny, a funny story that was true, and a true story that ended, as all true stories should, with laughter, with love, and with a door, open, waiting, for whoever comes next.
